explanation: Sitting upright promotes optimal alignment of the pharynx and esophagus, making swallowing easier and reducing aspiration risks. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h2)

question: What anatomical landmarks are used to measure the correct insertion length of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Mouth to neck to pubic bone
options.B: Nose to earlobe to xiphoid process
options.C: Nose to sternum to clavicle
options.D: Earlobe to jawline to umbilicus

explanation: This traditional measurement estimates the distance from the nares through the esophagus to the stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h3)

question: What action is required if a patient turns blue and coughs violently during tube insertion?

options.A: Inflate the internal retention balloon
options.B: Push the tube in faster
options.C: Immediately withdraw the tube
options.D: Give the patient more water

explanation: Coughing and cyanosis indicate that the tube has entered the airway instead of the esophagus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is considered the single most reliable method for verifying nasogastric tube placement?

options.A: Auscultating over the stomach
options.B: Measuring external tube length daily
options.C: Abdominal X-ray confirmation
options.D: Checking for condensation in the tube

explanation: Radiographic imaging provides clear visualization of the tube tip inside the stomach, eliminating guesswork. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why is auscultating air over the epigastric region discouraged as a standalone verification method?

options.A: Injecting air into the stomach causes immediate vomiting
options.B: Patients find listening with a stethoscope very uncomfortable
options.C: Air sounds similar whether the tube is in the stomach or lungs
options.D: The sound of air entry can be heard even when the tube is misplaced

explanation: Air pushed into the pharynx or lungs can create sounds similar to gastric entry, leading to false confidence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h4)

question: What common complication is prevented by careful taping of the nasogastric tube to the nose?

options.A: Nasal mucosal necrosis
options.B: Rapid electrolyte loss
options.C: Severe gastric bleeding
options.D: Chronic lower back pain

explanation: Constant pressure from an unsecured or tightly pulled tube against the nasal cartilage reduces blood flow, causing tissue breakdown. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why is frequent mouth care essential for a patient with a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Mouth breathing leads to dry, cracked mucous membranes
options.B: Oral bacteria travel up the tube into the stomach
options.C: Tooth decay occurs faster when gastric juices are present
options.D: Saliva production increases to digest the plastic material

explanation: Because the nose is partially blocked by the tube, patients breathe through the mouth, causing painful dryness. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h5)

question: At what angle should the bed be elevated during nasogastric tube feeding?

options.A: 0 degrees flat
options.B: 90 degrees upright
options.C: 15 degrees slight tilt
options.D: 30 to 45 degrees

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to keep formula and stomach contents from flowing back into the esophagus and lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the purpose of flushing a nasogastric tube with water before and after giving medications?

options.A: Preventing tube blockage from drug residue
options.B: Stimulating the stomach to produce acid
options.C: Cooling down hot liquid medications
options.D: Diluting the medication for faster absorption

explanation: Undissolved particles stick to the lumen and dry out, quickly clogging the narrow tube. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the proper initial step when a nasogastric tube becomes clogged during a feeding?

options.A: Inject carbonated soda and clamp the tube for hours
options.B: Replace the entire tube immediately without checking
options.C: Insert a metal guide wire to push the blockage out
options.D: Flush gently with warm water using a push-pause motion

explanation: Warm water and gentle pressure dissolve and dislodge most clogs safely without damaging the tube or injuring the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h7)

question: What does sudden nausea and vomiting in a patient with a nasogastric tube most likely indicate?

options.A: Delayed gastric emptying or tube displacement
options.B: Too much air being suctioned from the lungs
options.C: Allergic reaction to the plastic tube material
options.D: Normal adjustment to continuous liquid diet

explanation: If food stays in the stomach too long or the tube slips upward, gastric contents back up and cause vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is the patient instructed to hold their breath while the nasogastric tube is being removed?

options.A: To relax the abdominal muscles completely
options.B: To reduce the sensation of nasal tickling
options.C: To increase blood pressure during removal
options.D: To close the glottis and prevent aspiration

explanation: Holding the breath closes the airway, protecting the lungs from any fluid remaining in the tube as it passes the throat. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h8)

question: What is the correct way to handle the tube while pulling it out of the nose?

options.A: Kink or pinch the tube firmly
options.B: Pull it out very slowly over five minutes
options.C: Attach a heavy syringe to the tip
options.D: Leave the end completely open

explanation: Pinching the tube prevents any trapped residual fluid from spilling out into the pharynx or onto the patient's face. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h8)

question: What is the medical term for releasing intestinal gas through the anus?

options.A: Flatulence
options.B: Dyspepsia
options.C: Eructation
options.D: Halitosis

explanation: Flatulence refers specifically to the passage of gas from the digestive system out through the rectum and anus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why do patients usually seek medical care for flatulence?

options.A: Social embarrassment and disruptive symptoms
options.B: Immediate danger of bowel perforation
options.C: Severe systemic blood infection
options.D: Total inability to digest proteins

explanation: Patients typically consult healthcare providers when the gas volume or odor disrupts their daily activities and causes distress. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h1)

question: What are the two main sources of gas in the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: Gastric acid and pancreatic enzyme mixing
options.B: Swallowed air and bacterial fermentation
options.C: Bile breakdown and water reabsorption
options.D: Hepatic filtration and cellular respiration

explanation: Gastrointestinal gas comes from air a person swallows and gases produced by bacteria breaking down food in the gut. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which gas is primarily produced by colonic bacteria fermenting unabsorbed food?

options.A: Neon
options.B: Helium
options.C: Chlorine
options.D: Hydrogen

explanation: Colonic bacteria release hydrogen, methane, and carbon dioxide as they break down carbohydrates that the small intestine failed to absorb. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which food group is most commonly responsible for excessive colonic gas production?

options.A: Soluble proteins in plain egg whites
options.B: Saturated fats in red meat
options.C: Oligosaccharides in beans and cabbage
options.D: Simple sugars in table syrup

explanation: Beans and cabbage contain complex sugars that resist normal digestion, leaving them available for gas-producing bacteria in the colon. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h3)

question: A patient who eats very quickly is at risk for excess gas due to which mechanism?

options.A: Triggering rapid pancreatic enzyme release
options.B: Stopping all normal stomach acid production
options.C: Swallowing larger amounts of air
options.D: Speeding up total bowel transit time

explanation: Eating or drinking quickly causes aerophagia, which means swallowing extra air that eventually travels through the digestive tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is a common physical symptom that frequently accompanies excessive flatulence?

options.A: Unilateral facial weakness
options.B: Persistent high fever
options.C: Abdominal distension
options.D: Jaundice of the skin

explanation: Trapped gas inside the intestines often leads to visible swelling, bloating, and cramping pain in the abdomen. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h4)

question: What should a nurse focus on first when assessing a patient with severe flatulence?

options.A: Dietary history and bowel elimination patterns
options.B: Immediate scheduling for major abdominal surgery
options.C: Checking visual acuity and cranial nerves
options.D: Testing for rare genetic metabolic disorders

explanation: Reviewing what the patient eats and how their bowels function provides direct clues about the origin of excess gas. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which nursing intervention helps move trapped gas through the intestines by stimulating peristalsis?

options.A: Keeping the patient strictly on bed rest
options.B: Encouraging light physical walking
options.C: Applying ice packs to the chest
options.D: Restricting all fluid intake completely

explanation: Physical movement like walking stimulates intestinal motility, helping to pass trapped gas and relieve bloating. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h5)

question: How does chewing food thoroughly help reduce flatulence?

options.A: It prevents any bacteria from living in the colon
options.B: It breaks down food better and lowers swallowed air
options.C: It forces the liver to produce more bile salts
options.D: It completely stops the stomach from making acid

explanation: Thorough chewing eases digestion and prevents excess air intake that happens when gulping down poorly chewed meals. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is a useful tool for a patient trying to identify individual gas triggers?

options.A: Counting daily steps with a watch
options.B: Measuring daily body temperature
options.C: Tracking nighttime sleeping hours
options.D: Keeping a detailed food diary

explanation: A food diary allows patients to record what they eat and match it against episodes of excessive gas or bloating. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which beverage choice is best for a patient trying to reduce gastrointestinal gas?

options.A: Plain water
options.B: Chilled sparkling juice
options.C: Sweetened energy drinks
options.D: Carbonated soda

explanation: Plain water lacks the dissolved carbon dioxide gas found in carbonated drinks, which directly adds to intestinal gas volume. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a red flag symptom that requires prompt medical evaluation?

options.A: Unexplained and rapid weight loss
options.B: Presence of blood in the stool
options.C: Occasional burping after a large meal
options.D: Severe and worsening abdominal pain

explanation: Occasional burping or passing gas after eating is a normal physiological response, whereas weight loss and bleeding are red flags. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h7)

question: Why are symptoms like rectal bleeding and weight loss concerning when paired with gas?

options.A: They show that the patient eats too much fiber
options.B: They indicate normal aging changes in the colon
options.C: They prove the patient is drinking too much water
options.D: They suggest serious underlying organic pathology

explanation: Bleeding and weight loss point toward conditions like bowel inflammation or obstruction rather than simple dietary gas. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T10#GNS212_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of inserting a flatus tube?

options.A: To administer continuous rectal medications
options.B: To collect stool samples for laboratory analysis
options.C: To deliver liquid nutrition directly to the colon
options.D: To relieve severe abdominal distension from trapped gas

explanation: A flatus tube creates an open channel through the anal sphincter to let trapped intestinal gas escape and relieve pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h1)

question: When should a nurse consider using a flatus tube for a patient?

options.A: As the very first step for any mild post-operative gas pain
options.B: Before trying simple repositioning techniques in bed
options.C: After non-invasive measures like early ambulation fail to work
options.D: Whenever a patient requests relief from normal flatulence

explanation: Tubing is an invasive intervention kept for when simple actions like walking or shifting position do not clear trapped gas. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which clinical condition is an absolute contraindication for flatus tube insertion?

options.A: Early stage paralytic ileus
options.B: Recent rectal or anal surgery
options.C: Prolonged bed rest in adults
options.D: Mild post-operative flatulence

explanation: Inserting a tube over fresh surgical stitches can break sutures, open wounds, and cause severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is a bleeding disorder a major risk factor for this procedure?

options.A: Coagulation defects stop the tube from passing through the sphincter
options.B: Blood thinners make the intestinal gas expand much faster
options.C: The rectal mucosa is easily traumatized and prone to hemorrhage
options.D: Clotting problems completely block the release of trapped air

explanation: The delicate lining of the rectum can easily bleed if scraped by the tube, which is dangerous for patients who cannot clot well. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h2)

question: What type of lubricant must be used when preparing a flatus tube?

options.A: Alcohol-based gel
options.B: Water-soluble lubricant
options.C: Petroleum jelly base
options.D: Mineral oil ointment

explanation: Water-soluble lubricants are safe for mucous membranes and reduce friction without damaging rubber or plastic medical tubing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is a waterproof pad placed under the patient's hips before starting?

options.A: To elevate the pelvis for easier insertion into the rectum
options.B: To protect the bed linens from accidental stool leakage
options.C: To keep the patient warm during the entire procedure
options.D: To absorb any excess water-soluble gel used on the skin

explanation: Releasing gas often expels liquid stool along with it, so a pad prevents soiling the bed and saves time on linen changes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is the best patient position for inserting a flatus tube?

options.A: High Fowler's sitting pose
options.B: Supine with legs flat out
options.C: Left lateral Sims' position
options.D: Prone flat on the belly

explanation: The left lateral Sims' position matches the natural curve of the lower bowel, which eases insertion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why is explaining the procedure beforehand important for this task?

options.A: It prevents the patient from moving their legs during insertion
options.B: It stops the bowel from producing any more gas bubbles
options.C: It legally waives the need for a signed written consent form
options.D: It reduces anxiety and helps the patient relax their sphincter

explanation: Explaining what to expect calms the patient, reducing tension in the anal sphincter which makes the tube pass easier. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h4)

question: How far should a flatus tube be inserted into an adult patient?

options.A: 30 to 40 centimeters
options.B: 20 to 25 centimeters
options.C: 7 to 10 centimeters
options.D: 1 to 2 centimeters

explanation: Advancing the tube 7 to 10 centimeters ensures it safely enters the rectum past the anal sphincter without reaching the sigmoid colon. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h5)

question: What action must a nurse take if resistance is felt while advancing the tube?

options.A: Inject warm water to clear the blockage
options.B: Twist the tube quickly to break the barrier
options.C: Apply more pressure to push past the block
options.D: Stop immediately and do not force it

explanation: Forcing a rectal tube can cause severe trauma or perforation of the bowel wall. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the maximum recommended time a flatus tube should usually remain in place?

options.A: 2 to 4 hours
options.B: 12 to 24 hours
options.C: Over 48 hours
options.D: 20 to 30 minutes

explanation: Leaving a tube in for longer periods can press against the rectal lining and cut off blood supply, leading to tissue damage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is checking the abdomen after tube removal an essential nursing duty?

options.A: To confirm that abdominal distension and gas pressure have decreased
options.B: To check if the bowel sounds have completely disappeared
options.C: To ensure the anal sphincter has permanently closed shut
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the gas that escaped the body

explanation: Checking the abdomen lets the nurse evaluate if the procedure successfully met its goal of relieving trapped gas. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to include in the nursing documentation for this procedure?

options.A: The exact cost of the plastic collection bag
options.B: The brand name and color of the lubricant used
options.C: Amount of gas expelled and patient tolerance
options.D: Names of all visitors present in the room

explanation: Charting must capture the clinical outcome of the procedure and how well the patient tolerated the intervention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h7)

question: When should the nurse report an incident directly to the doctor during this care?

options.A: Whenever the patient falls asleep after the procedure
options.B: After every routine removal of a clean flatus tube
options.C: When normal soft stool appears on the waterproof pad
options.D: If bright red bleeding or severe pain occurs

explanation: Bleeding and severe pain are red flags indicating mucosal injury or improper insertion that needs immediate medical review. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing gastric lavage on a patient?

options.A: To measure accurate daily fluid balance in surgical wards
options.B: To collect routine baseline blood samples from the stomach
options.C: To provide long-term nutritional support for unconscious clients
options.D: To cleanse the stomach contents after toxic ingestion

explanation: Gastric lavage is specifically designed to wash out the stomach and remove unabsorbed poisons or drugs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h1)

question: When is gastric lavage most effective for a patient who ingested a poison?

options.A: Only after the patient develops chronic renal failure
options.B: Several days after the toxic substance was swallowed
options.C: Immediately or within a very short window after ingestion
options.D: Whenever the nurse notices mild abdominal distension

explanation: The procedure relies on catching the substance before it passes into the small intestine where absorption accelerates. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is gastric lavage strictly avoided after a patient swallows a corrosive acid?

options.A: It prevents the doctor from prescribing standard oral painkillers
options.B: It neutralizes the stomach acid and stops digestion permanently
options.C: It always causes permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: It risks causing a perforation of the damaged esophagus

explanation: Corrosive substances weaken tissue integrity, meaning passing a tube can easily rupture the esophagus or stomach wall. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which substance ingestion makes gastric lavage a dangerous contraindication due to aspiration risks?

options.A: Hydrocarbon solvents like kerosene
options.B: Common table salt dissolved in water
options.C: Pure sterile normal saline solution
options.D: Oral rehydration salts mixture

explanation: Kerosene and similar hydrocarbons easily enter the lungs during vomiting or tube removal, causing severe chemical pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h2)

question: What type of tube is preferred for emergency gastric lavage to clear pill fragments?

options.A: A rigid central venous catheter
options.B: A standard intravenous cannula
options.C: A tiny pediatric feeding tube
options.D: A large-bore orogastric tube

explanation: Small tubes easily clog with solid pill remnants, making a large-bore tube necessary for effective washing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why must a suction machine be prepared at the bedside before starting gastric lavage?

options.A: To test the electrical power socket before connecting equipment
options.B: To inflate the stomach with air prior to inserting the lavage tube
options.C: To pull out the gastric lining for routine laboratory biopsy
options.D: To clear the airway immediately if the patient vomits and aspirates

explanation: Vomiting during tube insertion or washing poses a severe aspiration risk, requiring instant airway suctioning. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why is an unconscious patient intubated with a cuffed tube before gastric lavage?

options.A: To protect the airway and prevent aspiration of stomach contents
options.B: To help the patient swallow the large gastric tube much faster
options.C: To measure the exact temperature of the lungs during the procedure
options.D: To stop the patient from talking while the nurse works

explanation: An unprotected airway in an unconscious client allows washed fluid or vomit to flood the lungs during lavage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the best patient position for performing a safe gastric lavage?

options.A: High Fowler position sitting straight upright in bed
options.B: Flat on the back with the neck fully hyperextended
options.C: Prone position resting flat on the stomach chest
options.D: Left lateral decubitus with head slightly lowered

explanation: This specific position slows gastric emptying into the intestines and helps pool fluid away from the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h4)

question: A nurse is performing gastric lavage and notices the return fluid contains heavy particulate matter. What action should be taken next?

options.A: Remove the tube immediately and document that the procedure is finished
options.B: Raise the patient into a standing position to speed up fluid removal
options.C: Continue cycling fluid aliquots until the return runs completely clear
options.D: Inject a large dose of intravenous antidote directly into the funnel

explanation: Lavage must continue until the effluent is clear to ensure all removable toxins are successfully extracted. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h5)

question: How should the nurse check that the lavage tube is inside the stomach before pouring fluid?

options.A: Immerse the outer end of the tube inside a glass of water
options.B: Check if the radial pulse rate increases suddenly
options.C: Ask the patient to count aloud from one to ten
options.D: Auscultate injected air over the epigastric region

explanation: Listening with a stethoscope over the stomach while injecting a bolus of air confirms correct placement. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why is normal saline preferred over plain tap water for gastric lavage in children?

options.A: To make the returning fluid look clear much faster
options.B: To prevent the tube from sticking to the stomach walls
options.C: To prevent dangerous electrolyte imbalances and water intoxication
options.D: To add extra calories to the stomach during the washing process

explanation: Plain water can be absorbed across the gastric mucosa, leading to severe hyponatremia and fluid overload, especially in smaller bodies. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h6)

question: What essential action must the nurse perform right before withdrawing the lavage tube?

options.A: Flush the tube with five liters of cold fruit juice
options.B: Pinch or fold the tube to prevent fluid aspiration
options.C: Disconnect the patient from all cardiac monitoring leads
options.D: Pump air rapidly down the tube to inflate the bowel

explanation: Pinching the tube traps any residual fluid inside, stopping it from spilling into the pharynx as the tube passes the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h6)

question: What complication can occur due to excessive vagal nerve stimulation during gastric tube insertion?

options.A: Cardiac arrhythmias or a sudden drop in heart rate
options.B: Sudden permanent blindness in both eyes
options.C: Complete paralysis of the upper extremities
options.D: Uncontrollable weight gain over several days

explanation: Passing a tube through the pharynx stimulates the vagus nerve, which can slow the heart rate or provoke dangerous rhythm changes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which symptom strongly suggests that gastric lavage has caused an accidental esophageal perforation?

options.A: Dry skin on the forehead and forearms
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the palms and soles
options.C: A temporary mild increase in the patient's appetite
options.D: Sudden severe chest or abdominal pain with bleeding

explanation: Tearing the esophagus or stomach wall causes sharp pain, localized trauma, and blood-stained returns. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a rectal washout in clinical practice?

options.A: To inflate the large intestine for a diagnostic X-ray image
options.B: To measure the exact core body temperature of the patient
options.C: To deliver systemic medications directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To thoroughly flush out the lower bowel and remove impacted stool

explanation: A rectal washout uses fluid to clean and clear out accumulated waste or meconium from the lower colon. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why is a rectal washout commonly performed in neonates with Hirschsprung's disease?

options.A: To close an abnormal opening in the abdominal wall
options.B: To permanently cure the underlying genetic bowel defect
options.C: To clear impacted meconium caused by a lack of nerve cells
options.D: To stimulate rapid weight gain and improve infant nutrition

explanation: The absence of ganglion cells stops normal movement, requiring a washout to remove trapped meconium. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h1)

question: A neonatal condition that frequently requires a rectal washout is...

options.A: neonatal jaundice
options.B: congenital heart failure
options.C: meconium plug syndrome
options.D: respiratory distress syndrome

explanation: Newborns with meconium plug syndrome cannot pass their first stool easily, making a washout necessary. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h2)

question: When is a rectal washout preferred over an oral bowel preparation?

options.A: When the patient requires complete cleansing of the entire small intestine
options.B: When the patient is fully conscious and eager to drink large volumes
options.C: When there is an active and severe infection in the stomach
options.D: When the patient cannot safely take medications or fluids by mouth

explanation: Rectal washouts bypass the upper gastrointestinal tract, making them ideal for patients unable to tolerate oral preparations. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which condition represents an absolute contraindication for a rectal washout?

options.A: Suspected acute bowel perforation
options.B: Mild chronic constipation
options.C: Uncomplicated internal hemorrhoids
options.D: Controlled essential hypertension

explanation: Introducing fluid into a perforated bowel pushes contents into the abdomen, causing severe infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is the best patient position for performing a rectal washout?

options.A: Supine with legs elevated high
options.B: Left lateral Sims position
options.C: Prone flat on the abdomen
options.D: High Fowler sitting upright

explanation: The left lateral position follows the natural curve of the lower bowel for easier fluid entry. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why must the washout fluid be warmed to body temperature before use?

options.A: To speed up the chemical dissolution of hard fecal masses
options.B: To ensure the fluid remains sterile inside the irrigation bag
options.C: To prevent abdominal cramping caused by cold temperature shock
options.D: To kill any bacteria present in the normal saline solution

explanation: Cold fluid triggers reflex bowel spasms and pain, making the procedure difficult to tolerate. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h4)

question: What type of lubricant should always be used on the catheter tip?

options.A: Antibiotic skin ointment
options.B: Petroleum jelly base
options.C: Water-soluble lubricant
options.D: Sterile mineral oil

explanation: Water-soluble gels protect delicate mucosal tissues and dissolve easily without harming the bowel. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h5)

question: What should the nurse do immediately if resistance is felt while advancing the catheter?

options.A: Quickly infuse a large volume of fluid to clear the block
options.B: Rotate the catheter rapidly to break up the resistance
options.C: Apply gentle physical force to push past the obstruction
options.D: Stop advancing immediately and investigate the cause

explanation: Forcing a catheter against resistance can easily cause a traumatic tear or bowel perforation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h5)

question: What critical calculation must be performed during and after a rectal washout?

options.A: Body mass index and surface area
options.B: Total daily caloric intake needs
options.C: Estimated glomerular filtration rate
options.D: Fluid balance of input versus output

explanation: Tracking fluid in and out ensures the patient is not retaining excessive fluid, which causes water intoxication. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which symptom in a newborn after a washout suggests possible vagal nerve overstimulation?

options.A: High fever and uncontrollable crying
options.B: Sudden excessive weight gain
options.C: Hyperactive bowel sounds everywhere
options.D: Sudden bradycardia and pale skin

explanation: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the vagus nerve, causing a drop in heart rate and pale, clammy skin. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which detail is NOT necessary to include in the rectal washout documentation?

options.A: The patient's tolerance of the procedure
options.B: The total volume of fluid instilled
options.C: The color and consistency of effluent
options.D: The brand name of the lubricant used

explanation: Specific commercial brand names of routine supplies are clinically irrelevant for charting patient outcomes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the primary legal and professional reason for documenting nursing care accurately?

options.A: It allows the billing department to charge extra fees for specialized equipment
options.B: It prevents the hospital from ever facing patient complaints or lawsuits
options.C: It guarantees that the patient will recover faster from the primary illness
options.D: It creates a reliable legal record that care was safely and correctly provided

explanation: Medical records serve as legal proof of the nursing interventions performed and the patient's response. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the primary anatomical purpose of creating a colostomy?

options.A: Increasing water absorption in the small intestine
options.B: Rerouting fecal matter through the abdominal wall
options.C: Restoring normal sphincter control after rectal surgery
options.D: Permanently curing chronic inflammatory bowel disease

explanation: A colostomy creates a surgical opening to divert stool away from a diseased or injured lower bowel segment. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: A patient with a gunshot wound to the abdomen most likely needs a colostomy for which reason?

options.A: Palliative care for advanced colon cancer
options.B: Long-term management of congenital anomalies
options.C: Emergency bowel perforation management
options.D: Correction of chronic malabsorption syndrome

explanation: Trauma injuries like gunshot wounds often cause bowel perforation, requiring rapid surgical diversion to prevent peritonitis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which type of colostomy produces liquid and highly irritating stool?

options.A: Ascending colostomy
options.B: Descending colostomy
options.C: Transverse colostomy
options.D: Sigmoid colostomy

explanation: An ascending colostomy is located high in the bowel tract, resulting in liquid output containing active digestive enzymes that easily irritate skin. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is the output of a sigmoid colostomy typically solid and formed?

options.A: Bile salts are completely absent from the digestive tract
options.B: Dietary fiber intake is strictly restricted postoperatively
options.C: The surgical procedure removes the entire large intestine
options.D: Most water absorption has already occurred in the colon

explanation: As waste travels through the entire length of the colon before reaching the sigmoid section, maximum water reabsorption takes place, solidifying the stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the expected appearance of a healthy, viable intestinal stoma?

options.A: Dark purple with a smooth surface
options.B: Pale, dry, and cool to touch
options.C: Pink to red and moist
options.D: White and completely flat with skin

explanation: A healthy stoma has a rich blood supply, making it appear pink or red and moist, similar to the mucous membrane inside the mouth. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: A newly formed stoma appears dark purple and dry during the morning shift assessment. What action should the nurse take first?

options.A: Document the finding as normal postoperative swelling
options.B: Notify the surgeon immediately regarding compromised blood supply
options.C: Irrigate the stoma gently with sterile normal saline
options.D: Apply a hydrocolloid powder to absorb excess moisture

explanation: A dark purple, dusky, or black stoma indicates ischemia or necrosis, which is a surgical emergency requiring immediate provider notification. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: How much skin should remain exposed between the stoma and the cut edge of the barrier?

options.A: One to two centimeters
options.B: At least half an inch
options.C: One to two millimeters
options.D: Zero millimeters, touching tightly

explanation: A small gap of one to two millimeters prevents the adhesive barrier from cutting into the stoma while protecting the surrounding skin from corrosive effluent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why is it important to gently push down on the newly applied skin barrier for about thirty seconds?

options.A: It forces trapped air bubbles out of the stomal lumen
options.B: Body heat activates the pressure-sensitive adhesive for a secure seal
options.C: Continuous pressure stops minor postoperative stomal bleeding
options.D: It flattens out normal postoperative abdominal wall creases

explanation: Gentle pressure and body warmth help the adhesive backing conform tightly to skin contours, preventing leaks. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which food item places a patient with a colostomy at the highest risk for a mechanical bowel blockage?

options.A: Popcorn
options.B: Steamed fish
options.C: Mashed yam
options.D: White rice

explanation: High-fiber, poorly digestible items like popcorn, nuts, and corn kernels easily lodge in the stoma opening, causing a blockage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: What dietary advice should a nurse give a patient troubled by excessive stoma gas?

options.A: Avoid carbonated drinks and chewing gum
options.B: Eliminate all dairy products from the diet
options.C: Drink less fluid during mealtimes
options.D: Increase intake of raw cabbage and beans

explanation: Swallowing air through gum chewing or consuming carbonated beverages directly increases gas production in the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: What term describes the abnormal sinking of the stoma below the level of the abdominal wall?

options.A: Parastomal hernia
options.B: Stomal retraction
options.C: Stomal prolapse
options.D: Stomal necrosis

explanation: Retraction occurs when the stoma pulls inward below skin level, making pouching difficult and causing severe leakage issues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which clinical finding is most indicative of a parastomal hernia?

options.A: A visible bulge around the stoma site when straining
options.B: Continuous bright red bleeding from the stoma tip
options.C: Complete absence of fecal output for forty-eight hours
options.D: Sudden black discoloration of the mucosal tissue

explanation: A parastomal hernia is a type of incisional hernia where abdominal contents push through the weakened muscle layer surrounding the stoma, creating a noticeable bulge. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is the best initial approach when teaching a newly admitted patient how to care for their colostomy?

options.A: Ask family members to take over all care permanently
options.B: Wait until discharge day to demonstrate the pouch change
options.C: Encourage them to look at and touch the stoma gradually
options.D: Provide a complex manual to read independently overnight

explanation: Gradual exposure helps patients overcome anxiety and body image distress, fostering self-reliance at a comfortable pace. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: Which resource is most valuable for helping a patient adjust emotionally to life with a permanent colostomy?

options.A: Stoma support groups and peer visitors
options.B: High-dose anti-anxiety medications
options.C: Advanced surgical textbooks on bowel resection
options.D: Strict dietary restriction handbooks

explanation: Interacting with individuals successfully living with a colostomy provides powerful reassurance and practical coping strategies. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: What part of the urinary system is responsible for filtering metabolic wastes from the blood?

options.A: Ureters
options.B: Urethra
options.C: Urinary bladder
options.D: Kidneys

explanation: The kidneys filter blood to remove waste products and excess fluid, forming urine in the process. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: What triggers the initial urge to urinate when the bladder fills?

options.A: Contraction of the external urethral sphincter
options.B: Increased pressure in the renal pelvis
options.C: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall
options.D: Direct stimulation from the renal cortex

explanation: As urine accumulates, stretch receptors in the bladder wall detect the volume change and send signals to the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: An adult patient producing less than 400 milliliters of urine per day has which condition?

options.A: Incontinence
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Retention
options.D: Oliguria

explanation: Oliguria is the medical term used to describe a significantly reduced urine output below normal daily thresholds. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: A patient reports experiencing sharp pain and burning whenever they pass urine. What is this symptom called?

options.A: Enuresis
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Hematuria
options.D: Dysuria

explanation: Dysuria refers to painful or burning urination, which frequently points to a urinary tract infection or irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the primary nursing responsibility when collecting a sample for a urine culture?

options.A: Use a sterile collection technique
options.B: Catheterize every patient routinely
options.C: Add chemical preservatives to the specimen bottle
options.D: Restrict all fluid intake prior to the test

explanation: A sterile technique prevents skin flora from contaminating the urine sample and skewing laboratory results. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why does the doctor order a serum creatinine test for a patient with urinary issues?

options.A: To evaluate overall renal function
options.B: To detect specific bacterial pathogens
options.C: To measure immediate bladder capacity
options.D: To check for urinary glucose levels

explanation: Serum creatinine measures waste products filtered by the kidneys, serving as a reliable indicator of kidney function. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is the main goal of establishing a timed voiding schedule for a patient with urinary retention?

options.A: To completely eliminate the need for fluid intake
options.B: To retrain bladder muscles and prevent overdistension
options.C: To increase the rate of red blood cell production
options.D: To prepare the patient for immediate surgery

explanation: Timed voiding encourages regular emptying, helping weakened bladder muscles regain tone and function. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: A bedridden patient has frequent episodes of urinary incontinence. What is the immediate nursing priority for skin care?

options.A: Massage the sacral area vigorously every two hours
options.B: Restrict fluid intake to keep the bed completely dry
options.C: Apply protective barrier creams to prevent skin breakdown
options.D: Leave the skin exposed to ambient air without cleaning

explanation: Urine exposure damages skin integrity quickly, making barrier creams and regular cleansing essential to prevent rashes and ulcers. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: Where should the urinary drainage bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Suspended from the overhead bed frame
options.B: Level with the patient's abdomen
options.C: Below the level of the bladder
options.D: Above the level of the bladder

explanation: Keeping the bag lower than the bladder uses gravity to prevent urine from flowing backward into the bladder and causing infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: Which nursing action is correct when providing daily hygiene for a patient with an indwelling catheter?

options.A: Push the catheter inward whenever crusts form
options.B: Disconnect the drainage tubing daily for deep cleaning
options.C: Apply antibiotic ointment liberally to the insertion site
options.D: Wash the meatal area gently with soap and water

explanation: Simple soap and water effectively remove secretions without irritating tissue or encouraging antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of teaching pelvic floor muscle exercises to a patient with incontinence?

options.A: To increase total bladder capacity
options.B: To decrease daily fluid production
options.C: To prevent kidney stone formation
options.D: To strengthen sphincter control

explanation: Kegel exercises tone the pelvic floor muscles, providing better support to the urethra and improving urinary control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: Which dietary item should a nurse advise a patient with bladder irritation to limit?

options.A: Caffeine
options.B: Plain water
options.C: Whole grains
options.D: Fresh vegetables

explanation: Caffeine acts as a bladder irritant and diuretic, which can worsen urgency and frequency symptoms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: What is the primary definition of urinary retention?

options.A: The inability to completely empty the bladder
options.B: The involuntary leakage of urine during coughing
options.C: The frequent passing of very small urine volumes
options.D: The total absence of urine production by kidneys

explanation: Urinary retention specifically refers to the body's inability to expel urine stored in the bladder, leading to incomplete emptying. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: How does urinary retention differ fundamentally from urinary incontinence?

options.A: Retention requires dialysis, while incontinence requires immediate surgery
options.B: Retention involves urine accumulation, while incontinence involves involuntary leakage
options.C: Retention causes painful urination, while incontinence is always painless
options.D: Retention affects only females, while incontinence affects only males

explanation: While both are common lower urinary tract disorders, retention is characterized by holding onto urine the body wants to expel, whereas incontinence is the uncontrolled loss of urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: A common mechanical obstruction causing urinary retention in older men is...

options.A: detrusor muscle weakness
options.B: anticholinergic medication use
options.C: benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.D: neurogenic bladder disease

explanation: Enlargement of the prostate gland physically squeezes the urethra, making it difficult for urine to pass out of the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: Why do certain drugs like antihistamines trigger urinary retention?

options.A: They cause the kidneys to produce excessive amounts of urine
options.B: They irritate the mucosal lining of the bladder wall
options.C: They impair the contraction of the detrusor muscle
options.D: They physically block the opening of the ureters

explanation: Many medications have anticholinergic properties that prevent the bladder muscle from squeezing strongly enough to empty properly. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: What is a defining feature of acute urinary retention?

options.A: Continuous dribbling of large urine volumes
options.B: Sudden onset with severe suprapubic pain
options.C: Gradual accumulation of urine without any pain
options.D: Completely normal bladder fullness on palpation

explanation: Acute retention hits abruptly and causes intense discomfort because the bladder distends rapidly over a short period. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why do patients with chronic urinary retention often experience overflow incontinence?

options.A: Frequent antibiotic use irritates the bladder lining and causes leakage
options.B: The kidneys suddenly start producing more urine than the bladder can hold
options.C: The urethral sphincter completely relaxes due to chronic nerve damage
options.D: The overstretched bladder leaks when intravesical pressure exceeds sphincter resistance

explanation: When a chronically full bladder reaches its limit, small amounts of urine escape past the tight sphincter, mimicking simple incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: What physical finding is most characteristic of a severely distended bladder?

options.A: A dull, rounded mass in the suprapubic region
options.B: A soft, flat abdomen with no tenderness on palpation
options.C: Sharp rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant
options.D: Hyperactive bowel sounds heard over the lower quadrants

explanation: A full bladder pushes upward out of the pelvis and presents as a palpable, dull-sounding mass just above the pubic bone. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: A male patient post-surgery cannot urinate for six hours and has lower belly pain. What is your immediate nursing assessment step?

options.A: Administer a strong oral diuretic medication as prescribed
options.B: Document the finding as normal post-operative urinary hesitancy
options.C: Palpate and perkuss the suprapubic area for bladder distention
options.D: Encourage the patient to drink two liters of water immediately

explanation: Checking for a palpable bladder confirms whether urine is actually accumulating before taking further clinical action. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: What non-invasive device is commonly used at the bedside to measure bladder volume?

options.A: Digital sphygmomanometer
options.B: Portable bladder ultrasound scanner
options.C: Peak flow respiratory meter
options.D: Standard multi-lead ECG machine

explanation: A bladder scanner calculates urine volume inside the bladder safely and quickly without inserting any tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: Why are serum creatinine and urea tests ordered for a patient with severe urinary retention?

options.A: To measure the exact volume of urine left inside the bladder
options.B: To calculate the correct dosage of antibiotics needed for treatment
options.C: To check if bladder backpressure has started harming the kidneys
options.D: To determine the specific bacterial infection causing the blockage

explanation: Longstanding high pressure in the urinary tract travels upward to the kidneys, impairing their filtration ability and elevating blood waste levels. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority treatment for acute urinary retention?

options.A: Immediate surgical removal of the prostate gland
options.B: Bladder decompression via catheterization
options.C: Continuous bladder irrigation with sterile water
options.D: Administration of high-dose intravenous diuretics

explanation: Relieving the agonizing pressure by draining accumulated urine through a catheter is the urgent first step. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: How do alpha-blockers help manage urinary retention caused by an enlarged prostate?

options.A: They dissolve the fibrous tissue obstructing the urethral lumen
options.B: They relax the smooth muscle fibers in the prostate and bladder neck
options.C: They stop the kidneys from making more urine during the night
options.D: They paralyze the bladder wall to stop painful muscle spasms

explanation: Alpha-blockers ease the squeeze around the urethra, allowing urine to flow more freely without immediate surgery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid draining a massive volume of urine all at once?

options.A: Total drainage stops the kidneys from producing any further urine
options.B: It forces air bubbles into the bladder and causes severe pain
options.C: Rapid decompression can cause bleeding and sudden blood pressure drops
options.D: It will immediately cause the catheter balloon to burst inside

explanation: Sudden reduction of intravesical pressure causes mucosal vessel rupture and rapid fluid shifts, risking shock and severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: You have inserted a catheter for acute retention and 1200 mL drains rapidly. What is your best action based on safety guidelines?

options.A: Inject sterile water into the balloon to secure the tubing in place
options.B: Clamp the tubing temporarily to control the rate of bladder decompression
options.C: Remove the catheter immediately and notify the doctor of the high volume
options.D: Administer a rapid intravenous fluid bolus to prevent dehydration

explanation: Gradual drainage prevents sudden pressure changes within the bladder and protects the patient from hemorrhage and shock. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is a severe systemic complication of untreated urinary retention?

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Urosepsis
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Stagnant, retained urine serves as a breeding ground for bacteria, which can easily invade the bloodstream and cause life-threatening sepsis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why is keeping the urinary drainage bag below the level of the bladder crucial?

options.A: It prevents backflow of contaminated urine into the bladder
options.B: It speeds up the rate of urine production by the kidneys
options.C: It keeps the catheter balloon inflated inside the bladder
options.D: It stops the patient from feeling the urge to urinate

explanation: Gravity ensures urine flows downward away from the body; lifting the bag above the bladder pushes bacteria straight back inside. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h8)

question: What is the primary clinical definition of urinary incontinence?

options.A: The involuntary loss of urine
options.B: Painful urination during the night
options.C: The complete inability to produce urine
options.D: An infection of the urinary bladder

explanation: Urinary incontinence is specifically defined as the involuntary leakage or loss of urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why do many elderly patients in Nigeria often fail to report urinary incontinence early?

options.A: Hospitals do not treat urinary tract issues
options.B: The symptoms disappear without medical treatment
options.C: Diagnostic tests are too expensive to perform
options.D: They consider it a normal part of aging

explanation: Many individuals delay seeking help because they mistakenly believe leaking urine is an inevitable part of growing older. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: Which part of the nervous system helps the bladder relax so it can store urine?

options.A: Somatic nervous system
options.B: Central nervous system
options.C: Sympathetic nervous system
options.D: Parasympathetic nervous system

explanation: The sympathetic nervous system promotes detrusor muscle relaxation and sphincter contraction so the bladder can hold urine safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: What happens in the bladder and urinary sphincter when a person urinates normally?

options.A: Both the detrusor and sphincter relax completely
options.B: Detrusor relaxation and sphincter contraction
options.C: Detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation
options.D: Both the detrusor and sphincter contract together

explanation: Urine leaves the body when the bladder muscle contracts while the outlet sphincter relaxes to open the passage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient leaks urine when coughing or lifting heavy market loads. What type of incontinence is this?

options.A: Stress urinary incontinence
options.B: Overflow urinary incontinence
options.C: Urge urinary incontinence
options.D: Functional urinary incontinence

explanation: Stress incontinence occurs when physical pressure from coughing or lifting overcomes weak pelvic floor muscles. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is the underlying mechanism responsible for overflow urinary incontinence?

options.A: Sudden bladder spasms without warning
options.B: Physical inability to walk to the toilet
options.C: Weakened pelvic floor support from childbirth
options.D: An overdistended bladder that fails to empty

explanation: Overflow incontinence occurs when urinary retention fills the bladder past capacity, causing continuous minor leakage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which condition is a major contributing factor to urinary incontinence in aging men?

options.A: Frequent pregnancies
options.B: Prostatic enlargement
options.C: Pelvic floor relaxation
options.D: Estrogen deficiency

explanation: Enlargement of the prostate gland obstructs the urinary outlet in men, frequently causing overflow or urge incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: How can chronic constipation contribute to urinary incontinence?

options.A: Hardened stool blocks the flow of urine in the urethra
options.B: The straining weakens the abdominal wall muscles permanently
options.C: Constipation causes severe dehydration and concentrated urine
options.D: Stool pressure in the rectum irritates the adjacent bladder

explanation: An impacted bowel exerts physical pressure against the urinary bladder, triggering involuntary bladder contractions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of a voiding diary during clinical assessment?

options.A: To measure the exact weight of the patient daily
options.B: To record fluid intake, leakage frequency, and triggers
options.C: To track the patient's daily diet and nutritional status
options.D: To calculate the total kidney filtration rate over time

explanation: A voiding diary helps nurses and doctors identify patterns, fluid habits, and specific triggers associated with leakage episodes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why is a urinalysis routinely performed during the evaluation of urinary incontinence?

options.A: To measure the exact bladder muscle thickness
options.B: To rule out active urinary tract infections
options.C: To assess the strength of the pelvic floor
options.D: To determine the patient's neurological status

explanation: Urinary tract infections can cause acute irritation and symptoms that mimic or worsen incontinence, so infection must be excluded. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the main goal of teaching a patient Kegel exercises?

options.A: To relax the abdominal wall
options.B: To empty the bowel completely
options.C: To reduce nighttime fluid intake
options.D: To strengthen pelvic floor muscles

explanation: Kegel exercises specifically target and strengthen the pelvic floor muscles to improve urinary sphincter control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: How does a timed voiding schedule help a patient with urge incontinence?

options.A: It eliminates the need for pelvic floor muscle training
options.B: It prevents the bladder from filling past the trigger point
options.C: It stretches the urethra to make passing urine easier
options.D: It completely stops the kidneys from producing urine

explanation: Scheduled voiding empties the bladder at regular intervals before unmanaged urgency and involuntary leakage can occur. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: Which class of medication is commonly prescribed to calm an overactive bladder muscle?

options.A: Anticholinergics
options.B: Diuretics
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: Anticholinergic drugs reduce bladder contractions and help manage symptoms of urge urinary incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why is topical estrogen sometimes prescribed for postmenopausal women with incontinence?

options.A: To increase the total volume of urine produced daily
options.B: To improve the health of urethral and vaginal tissues
options.C: To prevent the development of kidney stones
options.D: To stimulate voluntary contractions of the abdominal wall

explanation: Estrogen deficiency causes thinning of urogenital tissues, and topical application helps restore structural support and tissue health. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: What skin problem often happens when urine stays in contact with the skin for too long?

options.A: Increased production of subcutaneous fat
options.B: Complete loss of skin sensation
options.C: Permanent thickening of the epidermis
options.D: Moisture-associated skin breakdown

explanation: Constant exposure to urine irritates the skin, leading to rashes, sores, and moisture-associated skin breakdown. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: What should be the nurse's main focus when dealing with the emotional impact of incontinence?

options.A: Reducing social stigma and supporting patient dignity
options.B: Focusing solely on surgical treatment options
options.C: Ensuring the patient stays indoors at all times
options.D: Reporting the condition to public health authorities

explanation: Because patients often experience shame and isolation, nursing care must prioritize emotional support and dignity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: What triggers urine leakage in a patient with stress incontinence?

options.A: Physical pressure from activity
options.B: Complete blockage of the urethra
options.C: A severe urinary tract infection
options.D: Sudden bladder muscle spasms

explanation: Physical activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure force urine out when pelvic support is weak. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: How does stress incontinence differ from urge incontinence?

options.A: It only affects male patients rather than female patients
options.B: It occurs exclusively during sleep instead of waking hours
options.C: It is caused by physical pressure rather than sudden bladder muscle contractions
options.D: It involves complete inability to produce urine rather than leakage

explanation: Stress incontinence is a mechanical problem of support, while urge incontinence involves involuntary bladder muscle contractions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which muscle group forms the primary supportive sling for the pelvic organs?

options.A: Internal sphincter
options.B: Levator ani muscles
options.C: Abdominal rectus
options.D: Detrusor muscle

explanation: The levator ani group provides the main structural floor supporting the bladder and urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the urethral sphincters in urinary continence?

options.A: To remain contracted and keep the urinary channel closed at rest
options.B: To generate the force needed to empty the bladder completely
options.C: To transmit nerve signals from the spinal cord to the brain
options.D: To produce hormones that regulate daily urine production volume

explanation: Sphincters act as tight valves that maintain closure until purposeful urination occurs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is urethral hypermobility in the context of stress incontinence?

options.A: Complete rigidity of the urinary sphincter muscle fibers
options.B: Excessive downward movement of the bladder neck during pressure
options.C: Involuntary spasms of the bladder wall muscle
options.D: Rapid bacterial infection traveling up the urinary tract

explanation: Hypermobility means the support structures have slackened, allowing the urethra to drop abnormally during strain. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: Why does weakening of the pelvic floor lead directly to urine leakage?

options.A: It blocks the normal flow of blood to the bladder walls
options.B: It causes the bladder to shrink to a much smaller size
options.C: It prevents proper pressure transmission to close the urethra
options.D: It stops the kidneys from filtering waste products properly

explanation: Without a firm backstop from supportive tissues, increased abdominal pressure pushes urine out past the unsupported urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: Which factor is a primary cause of pelvic floor trauma leading to stress incontinence?

options.A: A sedentary lifestyle
options.B: High daily water intake
options.C: Consuming too much caffeine
options.D: Vaginal childbirth

explanation: The stretching and physical strain of vaginal delivery frequently damages pelvic support tissues and nerves. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: How does chronic coughing contribute to the development of stress incontinence?

options.A: By placing repetitive downward strain on the pelvic floor muscles
options.B: By increasing overall daily urine production in the kidneys
options.C: By irritating the inner lining of the urinary bladder
options.D: By weakening the nerve connections in the lower spinal cord

explanation: Repeated forceful coughs repeatedly stress and fatigue the pelvic support structures until they weaken. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: What is the purpose of a bladder diary during clinical assessment?

options.A: To measure exact muscle strength in the pelvic floor
options.B: To record daily fluid intake and episodes of leakage
options.C: To check blood pressure changes during urination
options.D: To test for bacterial infections in the urine sample

explanation: A bladder diary tracks patterns of fluid consumption and incontinence events over multiple days. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: How is a basic cough stress test performed during a physical exam?

options.A: The nurse listens to the abdomen with a stethoscope while coughing
options.B: The patient coughs with a full bladder while observing for leakage
options.C: The patient drinks large volumes of water until coughing starts
options.D: The patient holds their breath while running on a treadmill

explanation: Observing immediate urine loss during a cough confirms the mechanical nature of stress incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of teaching Kegel exercises to a patient?

options.A: To reduce nighttime urine production by the kidneys
options.B: To relax the abdominal wall during deep breathing exercises
options.C: To strengthen the pelvic floor muscles supporting the urethra
options.D: To expand the total physical capacity of the bladder muscle

explanation: Kegels build strength in the levator ani muscles to improve structural support around the urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which instruction is most important when teaching a patient how to perform Kegel exercises?

options.A: Hold your breath tightly for one full minute during each contraction
options.B: Perform the exercises only while standing up in front of a mirror
options.C: Drink two glasses of water immediately before starting your routine
options.D: Avoid contracting your abdominal, thigh, or buttock muscles at the same time

explanation: Isolating the pelvic floor ensures the correct muscle group is being strengthened without substituting other muscle groups. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is the most common surgical procedure performed for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Artificial kidney transplant
options.B: Complete bladder removal
options.C: Prostate gland resection
options.D: Mid-urethral sling placement

explanation: Mid-urethral slings provide a supportive hammock under the urethra to prevent downward displacement during pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: Why might a doctor prescribe topical estrogen to a postmenopausal patient with stress incontinence?

options.A: To stimulate rapid weight loss and reduce abdominal pressure
options.B: To improve the health and elasticity of the urethral tissues
options.C: To increase the total volume of urine held in the kidneys
options.D: To cause temporary paralysis of the bladder wall muscles

explanation: Estrogen helps maintain mucosal thickness and vascularity in the urogenital tissues, supporting closure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common complication associated with chronic untreated stress incontinence?

options.A: Severe perineal skin breakdown
options.B: Complete permanent kidney failure
options.C: Recurrent urinary tract infections
options.D: Social withdrawal and isolation

explanation: Stress incontinence affects lower urinary tract support, not kidney filtration function, so kidney failure is not a typical complication. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is a key nursing priority when educating a patient recovering from a mid-urethral sling procedure?

options.A: Telling them pelvic floor exercises are no longer necessary
options.B: Instructing them to stop drinking all fluids for three months
options.C: Encouraging heavy lifting immediately to test the new sling
options.D: Teaching them to watch for signs of urinary retention or infection

explanation: Postoperative monitoring for normal voiding and infection prevention is essential after urinary tract surgery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a medical bougie?

options.A: To widen strictures and guide tube placement
options.B: To irrigate blocked surgical drains continuously
options.C: To measure core body temperature accurately
options.D: To suture internal tissues during open surgery

explanation: Bougies are slender, flexible instruments designed to navigate narrow tracts, stretch strictures, and act as guides for larger therapeutic tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why must nurses understand the physical differences between bougies and dilators?

options.A: To bill the patient accurately for disposable hospital supplies
options.B: To select the correct instrument and prevent mucosal trauma
options.C: To calculate exact drug dosages based on instrument length
options.D: To sterilize the equipment using high-pressure steam autoclaves

explanation: Knowing the flexibility and rigidity of these devices ensures appropriate clinical application and protects fragile internal tissues from injury. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which type of bougie relies on heavy internal filling to assist with gravity-driven passage?

options.A: Hurst bougie
options.B: Savary-Gillard dilator
options.C: Maloney bougie
options.D: Urethral sound

explanation: Maloney bougies contain mercury or tungsten inside to provide weighted momentum during esophageal dilation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is the specific advantage of using a wire-guided Savary-Gillard dilator?

options.A: It delivers continuous electrical current to cauterize bleeding tissue
options.B: It safely tracks over a guidewire through tight strictures
options.C: It allows direct visualization through an attached miniature camera
options.D: It relies entirely on gravity without requiring manual pressure

explanation: Wire-guided systems reduce the risk of creating false passages by following the precise path established by a secure guidewire. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: A common gastrointestinal indication for using an esophageal dilator is:

options.A: Gastric ulceration
options.B: Peptic stricture
options.C: Acute appendicitis
options.D: Internal hemorrhoids

explanation: Chronic acid exposure leads to scar tissue formation and narrowing, known as a peptic stricture, which requires mechanical dilation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: A patient with chronic urethral strictures is admitted with painful urination and poor urine stream. What primary problem does dilation address?

options.A: Excessive production of concentrated urine
options.B: Obstruction to normal urinary elimination
options.C: Weakness of the external urinary sphincter
options.D: Bacterial colonization of the urinary bladder

explanation: Urethral strictures mechanically block urine flow, and dilating the tract relieves this obstruction to restore normal voiding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: What is the primary reason an adult patient must remain NPO before an esophageal dilation procedure?

options.A: To ensure accurate blood glucose level readings
options.B: To prevent pulmonary aspiration during the procedure
options.C: To prevent allergic reactions to local anesthetics
options.D: To allow complete absorption of oral medications

explanation: An empty stomach significantly reduces the risk of regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents during upper GI instrumentation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which nursing action is most critical during the immediate pre-procedure phase for a dilation?

options.A: Placing the patient in a prone position for airway drainage
options.B: Inserting a large-bore peripheral intravenous line in the foot
options.C: Administering a full dose of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
options.D: Verifying informed consent and checking baseline vital signs

explanation: Confirming consent ensures legal and ethical readiness, while baseline vitals provide essential reference points for monitoring procedural tolerance. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: What type of lubricant should the nurse prepare for inserting medical bougies or dilators?

options.A: Sterile mineral oil
options.B: Silicone-based gel
options.C: Petroleum-based ointment
options.D: Water-soluble lubricant

explanation: Water-soluble lubricants facilitate smooth insertion without damaging delicate medical polymers or leaving irritating oily residues inside tracts. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why is continuous pulse oximetry essential during an esophageal dilation procedure under sedation?

options.A: To determine when the local anesthetic has completely worn off
options.B: To measure the exact depth of the stricture inside the esophagus
options.C: To calculate the total volume of blood lost during insertion
options.D: To detect early signs of hypoxia or respiratory depression

explanation: Sedation combined with upper GI manipulation places the patient at risk for airway compromise, making oxygen saturation monitoring vital. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: What is the most serious potential complication following an esophageal or urethral dilation procedure?

options.A: Temporary hair loss
options.B: Peripheral edema
options.C: Tissue perforation
options.D: Hypertensive crisis

explanation: Mechanical stretching of tight strictures carries an inherent risk of tearing or perforating the mucosal wall, which is a surgical emergency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: A patient complains of sudden, severe chest pain and develops a fever two hours after an esophageal dilation. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Acute anxiety attack
options.B: Esophageal perforation
options.C: Normal post-procedure soreness
options.D: Mild local anesthetic reaction

explanation: Severe chest pain and fever post-procedure are classic indicators of a tear or perforation requiring urgent medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: Which instruction is most appropriate for a patient discharged after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: Progress slowly from clear liquids to soft foods as tolerated
options.B: Avoid drinking any fluids for at least forty-eight hours
options.C: Resume a regular spicy solid diet immediately upon arrival home
options.D: Lie flat in bed for two hours after every meal

explanation: Gradual dietary advancement prevents irritation and ensures the newly dilated esophagus can comfortably handle food intake. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: Why is it important to provide written discharge instructions to patients after a dilation procedure?

options.A: Patients may forget verbal instructions due to residual sedation or stress
options.B: Insurance companies mandate written proof of completed nursing care
options.C: It replaces the need for any verbal explanation by the nursing staff
options.D: Hospital policies require a signed paper copy for medical billing

explanation: Anxiety and lingering medication effects impair memory retention, making written guides essential for safe home recovery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: Which patient condition makes passing a nasogastric tube through the nose absolutely unsafe?

options.A: Basilar skull fracture
options.B: Mild confusion
options.C: Ischemic stroke
options.D: Diabetic ketoacidosis

explanation: Passing a tube through the nose in a patient with a skull fracture risks entering the intracranial vault. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is feeding through a nasogastric tube preferred over total parenteral nutrition when the digestive tract works?

options.A: It avoids the need for fluid balance charts
options.B: It requires less monitoring of blood glucose
options.C: It maintains intestinal mucosal integrity
options.D: It is completely free of infectious risks

explanation: Enteral feeding keeps the gut mucosa active, preventing atrophy and bacterial translocation from the bowel lumen. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: What is the standard tube size range for an adult nasogastric insertion?

options.A: 30 to 36 French
options.B: 14 to 16 French
options.C: 24 to 28 French
options.D: 6 to 8 French

explanation: Adults generally require a 14 to 16 Fr tube to allow adequate flow for feeding and decompression without excessive mucosal pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: Checking the patency of both nostrils before NG insertion helps the nurse decide what?

options.A: If the stomach is currently empty of contents
options.B: Which side has better airflow for safe passage
options.C: Whether the patient has a swallowing reflex
options.D: How much lubricant to apply to the tube tip

explanation: Assessing airflow and patency ensures the nurse chooses the clearest nostril, reducing trauma during insertion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does the letter E stand for in the NEX measurement method?

options.A: Eyebrow
options.B: Earlobe
options.C: Epiglottis
options.D: Esophagus

question: A patient coughs and turns dusky blue while you are advancing an NG tube. What action should you take?

options.A: Push the tube down faster
options.B: Withdraw the tube immediately
options.C: Give the patient water to drink
options.D: Listen over the chest with a stethoscope

question: What is considered the gold standard method for confirming nasogastric tube placement?

options.A: Abdominal X-ray
options.B: Observing cough reflex
options.C: Testing fluid pH
options.D: Auscultation of air

explanation: An abdominal X-ray gives visual proof of the exact anatomical location of the distal tube tip. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why is listening with a stethoscope over the stomach while pushing air not recommended anymore for checking tube placement?

options.A: It exposes the patient to dangerous levels of radiation
options.B: It causes severe trauma to the gastric mucosa
options.C: It requires specialized equipment that is rarely available
options.D: Air sounds can easily be transmitted from other areas

explanation: Injecting air can be heard over the epigastrium even when the tube is misplaced in the esophagus or lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the recommended minimum head-of-bed elevation during a nasogastric feeding?

options.A: 30 degrees
options.B: 90 degrees
options.C: Flat on back
options.D: 10 degrees
