explanation: Elevating the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees uses gravity to prevent reflux and pulmonary aspiration. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of flushing an NG tube with water before and after medication administration?

options.A: To prevent tube occlusion from drug residue
options.B: To stimulate normal bowel peristalsis
options.C: To provide total daily fluid requirements
options.D: To cool down warm liquid medications

explanation: Water flushes clear the narrow lumen of the tube, stopping medications from reacting and clogging the line. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: How can a nurse prevent pressure ulcers on the nares of a patient with an NG tube?

options.A: Remove the tube every shift for resting the skin
options.B: Lubricate the outside of the nostril with heavy ointment
options.C: Apply tight gauze wrapping around the bridge of the nose
options.D: Secure the tube properly and clean the nares daily

explanation: Daily cleaning and proper securing prevent the tube from pressing too hard against delicate nasal cartilage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: A patient receiving an NG feeding develops diarrhea. What is a common contributing factor?

options.A: Feeding administered too cold
options.B: Patient lying completely flat
options.C: Water flushes given too often
options.D: Tube placed in the left bronchus

explanation: Cold formula can cause gastrointestinal cramping and rapid transit, leading to diarrhea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why should a patient hold their breath during the removal of an NG tube?

options.A: To close the glottis and prevent aspiration
options.B: To decrease nasal mucosal bleeding
options.C: To relax the abdominal wall muscles
options.D: To prevent sudden episodes of vomiting

explanation: Holding the breath closes the airway, stopping any residual fluid in the tube from entering the trachea during extraction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: Which detail is most important to document right after successfully placing a new NG tube?

options.A: The total cost of the equipment consumed
options.B: The brand name of the feeding formula used
options.C: The external length measurement at the naris
options.D: The name of the assistant who held the light

explanation: Recording the exit mark lets future shifts quickly check if the tube has slipped inward or been pulled out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the approximate length of the adult female urethra?

options.A: 18 to 20 cm
options.B: 25 to 30 cm
options.C: 3.8 to 5 cm
options.D: 10 to 12 cm

explanation: The female urethra is significantly shorter than the male urethra, typically measuring between 3.8 and 5 centimeters. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why does the male urethra present a greater challenge during catheterisation compared to the female urethra?

options.A: It connects directly to the ureters without a bladder
options.B: It has multiple sections and natural curves
options.C: It possesses a much wider diameter throughout
options.D: It is surrounded by a weaker sphincter muscle

explanation: The male urethra is longer and includes prostatic, membranous, and penile sections with curves that require careful maneuvering during catheter passage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Which catheter type is designed for continuous bladder irrigation following urological surgery?

options.A: Single-lumen catheter
options.B: Intermittent catheter
options.C: Three-way catheter
options.D: Straight rubber catheter

explanation: A three-way indwelling catheter contains an extra channel dedicated to continuous fluid infusion for bladder irrigation and blood clot removal. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: A patient admitted with severe postpartum urinary retention requires bladder drainage without a prolonged indwelling device. What is the most appropriate equipment?

options.A: Three-way Foley catheter
options.B: Suprapubic catheter
options.C: Intermittent catheter
options.D: Condom catheter

explanation: Intermittent catheters are inserted for immediate drainage and removed right away, avoiding the infection risks associated with long-term indwelling tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: What allergy must be specifically checked before inserting a standard indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: Penicillin
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Latex
options.D: Sulfonamide

explanation: Many conventional catheters are manufactured from latex, making pre-procedural allergy screening vital to prevent severe hypersensitivity reactions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of explaining the catheterisation procedure to the patient beforehand?

options.A: To obtain legal permission from the hospital director
options.B: To reduce anxiety and encourage patient cooperation
options.C: To assess the patient's baseline renal function
options.D: To eliminate the need for sterile gloves during setup

explanation: Clear explanation promotes relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles, which makes urethral identification and catheter passage much easier. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: Why must the catheter be advanced a few centimeters further after urine first appears?

options.A: To ensure the balloon is fully inside the bladder before inflation
options.B: To prevent the drainage bag from filling up too quickly
options.C: To stretch the urethral sphincter for permanent dilation
options.D: To anchor the drainage tubing directly against the meatus

explanation: Inflating the retention balloon inside the urethra instead of the bladder causes severe trauma and intense pain for the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: During catheterisation of a male patient, resistance is met at the external sphincter. What action should the nurse take?

options.A: Apply maximum physical force to push past the obstruction
options.B: Inflate the retention balloon immediately at that exact spot
options.C: Withdraw the equipment and abandon all future attempts
options.D: Ask the patient to take slow deep breaths and gently pause

explanation: Deep breathing helps relax the pelvic floor and external sphincter, allowing the catheter to pass smoothly without forcing tissue. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: Where must the urine collection bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Hanging from the headboard
options.B: Directly level with the hips
options.C: Below the level of the bladder
options.D: Above the mattress surface

explanation: Gravity drainage requires the bag to remain lower than the bladder to prevent contaminated urine from flowing backward into the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for securing the catheter tubing to the patient's thigh?

options.A: To prevent accidental disconnection of the drainage bag
options.B: To minimize urethral trauma caused by traction and movement
options.C: To stop spontaneous deflation of the retention balloon
options.D: To accelerate the normal rate of glomerular filtration

explanation: Securing the tubing stops piston-like movement of the catheter inside the urethra, which reduces inflammation, erosion, and irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: How should a nurse manage sudden painful bladder spasms in a patient with a patent catheter?

options.A: Administer prescribed antispasmodic medications
options.B: Pull the catheter outward until resistance is met
options.C: Clamp the drainage tubing for four hours at a time
options.D: Inflate the retention balloon with extra sterile water

explanation: Bladder spasms are contractions of the detrusor muscle triggered by the foreign body; antispasmodics calm the muscle without altering the device. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: Which finding is most characteristic of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.A: Fever and cloudy urine
options.B: Increased urine specific gravity
options.C: Dark amber concentrated output
options.D: High systemic blood pressure

explanation: Infection in the urinary tract typically manifests with systemic signs like fever alongside turbid, foul-smelling urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: What tool is required to deflate the retention balloon prior to catheter removal?

options.A: A sterile clamp or hemostat
options.B: An intravenous infusion cannula
options.C: A luer-lock syringe without a needle
options.D: A surgical scalpel blade

explanation: A needleless syringe is inserted into the inflation valve to extract the sterile water used to keep the balloon inflated. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h7)

question: A patient has not voided eight hours after catheter removal and reports lower abdominal discomfort. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Re-insert a new indwelling catheter immediately without checking
options.B: Encourage the patient to restrict all fluid intake for the day
options.C: Administer a potent diuretic medication orally
options.D: Assess for bladder distention and notify the physician

explanation: Post-catheter urinary retention is a common complication requiring clinical assessment and possible re-catheterisation or bladder scanning. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h7)

question: What primary feature keeps an indwelling urinary catheter secured inside the bladder?

options.A: A retention balloon filled with sterile water
options.B: A suction mechanism connected to the drainage bag
options.C: An external adhesive tape attached to the thigh
options.D: A flexible wire mesh anchored to the urethral wall

explanation: Inflating the internal balloon with sterile water prevents the catheter from slipping out of the bladder prematurely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: A patient admitted to the surgical ward requires hourly urine output tracking. Why is an indwelling catheter chosen over intermittent catheterization?

options.A: Patients find indwelling tubes much more comfortable than periodic drainage
options.B: Indwelling catheters completely eliminate the risk of urinary tract infections
options.C: Continuous drainage allows real-time monitoring without repeated urethral trauma
options.D: Intermittent catheters cannot be used in male surgical patients

explanation: Continuous urine output monitoring in unstable patients requires an open, uninterrupted drainage pathway to assess kidney perfusion accurately. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: What is the approximate length of the adult female urethra?

options.A: 18 to 20 centimeters
options.B: 25 to 30 centimeters
options.C: 3 to 5 centimeters
options.D: 10 to 12 centimeters

explanation: The female urethra is short, measuring roughly 3 to 5 cm, which also places women at a higher risk for bacterial ascent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: A student nurse preparing to catheterize an elderly female patient cannot locate the urinary meatus due to tissue changes. What action should the nurse take next?

options.A: Reposition the patient into a Sims or lateral position for better exposure
options.B: Force the catheter upward until urine returns spontaneously
options.C: Insert the catheter blindly into the largest visible opening in the area
options.D: Abandon the procedure entirely without notifying the primary team

explanation: Altering the patient's position can bring hidden anatomical landmarks into view safely without risking accidental vaginal catheterization. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: What does a French (Fr) scale measurement represent regarding a urinary catheter?

options.A: The volume capacity of the retention balloon
options.B: The external diameter of the catheter tube
options.C: The maximum pressure threshold of the valve
options.D: The total length of the drainage tubing

explanation: The French scale measures catheter caliber, with larger numbers indicating thicker tube diameters. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: Why is a coude tip catheter specifically chosen for an older male patient with prostatic enlargement?

options.A: The integrated balloon requires no fluid for bladder retention
options.B: The wider lumen prevents clots from blocking the drainage channels
options.C: The soft silicone material dissolves automatically after two weeks
options.D: The curved tip helps navigate past the obstructed prostatic urethra

explanation: The upward curve of a coude tip glides smoothly over an enlarged prostate gland where straight catheters usually get stuck. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: What critical allergy must a nurse screen for before opening a standard catheterization kit?

options.A: Dietary proteins and gluten
options.B: Oral antibiotics and analgesics
options.C: Latex and antiseptic solutions
options.D: Intravenous fluids and saline

explanation: Standard trays often contain latex catheters and iodine-based antiseptics, both of which can provoke severe allergic responses. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why is it important to perform a bladder scan or abdominal palpation prior to catheterization?

options.A: To confirm the actual presence of urine retention before invasive manipulation
options.B: To stimulate voluntary micturition and avoid the procedure entirely
options.C: To measure the exact length of the urethral canal accurately
options.D: To determine if the patient has a systemic urinary tract infection

explanation: Assessing bladder volume prevents unnecessary catheterization in patients whose bladders are actually empty. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: When should the retention balloon be inflated during an indwelling catheter insertion?

options.A: Immediately upon touching the external urinary meatus
options.B: After urine flow is observed and the catheter is advanced further
options.C: After the drainage bag is completely filled with urine
options.D: Before inserting any portion of the tube into the urethral canal

explanation: Inflating the balloon inside the urethra causes severe trauma; it must rest entirely inside the bladder cavity first. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: A nurse inserts a catheter into a female patient, sees urine flow, and immediately inflates the balloon. The patient cries out in sharp pain. What mistake occurred?

options.A: The drainage bag was placed above the level of the bladder
options.B: A Coude tip catheter was selected instead of a straight one
options.C: The catheter was not advanced far enough before balloon inflation
options.D: The antiseptic solution used was far too cold for the patient

explanation: Seeing urine confirms the tip is in the bladder neck, but advancing further ensures the balloon clears the urethral sphincter before inflation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: Where must the urine collection bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Elevated on an IV pole during ambulation
options.B: Level with the patient's hips when sitting
options.C: Always below the level of the bladder
options.D: Hanging directly on the bed mattress surface

explanation: Gravity drainage fails and urine flows backward into the bladder if the collection bag is raised above bladder level. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: Why should nurses avoid applying antibacterial ointments around the catheter insertion site?

options.A: Creams instantly block the drainage eyes and cause acute retention
options.B: Lipid-based substances neutralize the effect of the sterile water balloon
options.C: Antimicrobial creams dissolve the silicone material of the catheter
options.D: Ointments trap moisture and can promote fungal or bacterial growth

explanation: Moisture barrier accumulation around the meatus creates an ideal breeding ground for pathogens rather than protecting against infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: What is the single most effective measure for preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infections?

options.A: Applying antibiotic cream to the meatus twice daily
options.B: Performing daily bladder washouts with sterile saline
options.C: Changing the entire drainage bag every twenty-four hours
options.D: Prompt removal of the catheter when clinically unnecessary

explanation: Limiting the duration of catheterization drastically reduces the window for bacterial colonization and biofilm formation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why is routine prophylactic bladder irrigation discouraged in patients with indwelling catheters?

options.A: Irrigation fluids instantly trigger severe bladder spasms and bleeding
options.B: Continuous flushing prevents the kidneys from producing normal urine
options.C: Saline solutions dissolve the rubber material of the drainage bag
options.D: Breaking the closed system increases the risk of introducing bacteria

explanation: Opening sealed drainage junctions defeats the closed-system barrier designed to keep external microbes out of the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: A patient with an indwelling catheter has had no urine output for three hours and reports lower abdominal fullness. What is the nurse's first action?

options.A: Immediately deflate the balloon and remove the catheter
options.B: Administer a potent loop diuretic intravenously
options.C: Disconnect the drainage bag to flush the catheter with tap water
options.D: Inspect the tubing for kinks, twists, or external pressure

explanation: Checking for simple mechanical obstructions like a kinked line or a patient lying on the tubing is always the first troubleshooting step. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the typical underlying cause of urine leaking around the insertion site of an indwelling catheter?

options.A: A failure to inflate the retention balloon with enough sterile water
options.B: Excessive daily fluid intake overwhelming the drainage bag capacity
options.C: The collection bag hanging too low below the level of the mattress
options.D: Bladder spasms causing the detrusor muscle to contract around the tube

explanation: Involuntary bladder contractions squeeze urine out past the catheter walls, resulting in bypassing or leakage around the meatus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What crucial step must be performed before pulling out an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: Apply antiseptic ointment directly to the external meatus
options.B: Flush the drainage lumen with sterile water to clear sediment
options.C: Completely deflate the retention balloon by withdrawing all fluid
options.D: Clamp the drainage tubing for two hours prior to extraction

explanation: Failing to remove all water from the balloon turns the catheter into a makeshift obstacle that severely tears the urethra during extraction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)

question: A patient's catheter is removed at 0800. By 1500, the patient feels lower abdominal discomfort and has not voided. What is the appropriate nursing assessment?

options.A: Encourage the patient to wait overnight before reporting symptoms
options.B: Administer an oral laxative to stimulate pelvic nerve pathways
options.C: Reinsert a new indwelling catheter immediately without evaluation
options.D: Assess for urinary retention using bladder palpation or scanning

explanation: Patients should void within 6 to 8 hours post-removal; failing this requires checking for urinary retention and potential bladder distension. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)

question: Why do surgeons place a surgical drain?

options.A: To close deep wounds faster
options.B: To prevent fluid from building up and causing infection
options.C: To stop the need for antibiotics
options.D: To help the body reabsorb blood

explanation: Drains stop blood, serum, or pus from pooling, which lowers the chance of bacteria growing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: When is a prophylactic drain used?

options.A: After an infection has already started
options.B: Before surgery to empty the bowel
options.C: To treat a confirmed internal abscess
options.D: During surgery to stop expected fluid buildup

explanation: Prophylactic drains are placed when a surgeon expects extra fluid or blood after an operation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of an open drainage system?

options.A: Chest drainage unit
options.B: Penrose drain
options.C: Jackson-Pratt drain
options.D: Hemovac reservoir

explanation: A Penrose drain is an open system that lets fluid drain straight onto dressings outside the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: Why are closed drainage systems preferred over open systems?

options.A: They lower the risk of germs traveling back into the body
options.B: They let fluid evaporate through the plastic
options.C: They mean nurses never need to check them
options.D: They do not rely on gravity

explanation: Sealed tubing stops environmental germs from easily moving backward into body tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is the main job of a nasogastric tube attached to suction?

options.A: Emptying fluid and gas from the stomach
options.B: Giving high-protein liquid feeds
options.C: Delivering medicine to the lungs
options.D: Checking continuous blood pressure

explanation: Suction through an NG tube clears out stomach contents to stop bloating, nausea, and vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why must a urine bag always hang lower than the patient's bladder?

options.A: To stop urine from flowing backward into the bladder
options.B: To keep pressure high in the tube
options.C: To help the kidneys make urine faster
options.D: To make it easier for the nurse to read without bending

explanation: Gravity keeps urine moving away from the body. Raising the bag causes urine to flow backward, which can lead to an infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: What does a sudden stop in fluid from a surgical drain usually mean?

options.A: The suction has naturally increased
options.B: The patient is completely healed
options.C: The tube is blocked or kinked
options.D: The body has stopped making fluid

explanation: A sudden drop in output is usually caused by a physical blockage in the tube rather than an overnight cure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: What should you do right away if bright red blood suddenly fills a surgical drain?

options.A: Clamp the drain so no more blood leaves
options.B: Lower the collection bag to the floor
options.C: Call the surgical team about possible bleeding
options.D: Flush the tube with sterile normal saline

explanation: Bright red bleeding points to active bleeding inside that needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: Why do you need to squeeze bulb-style suction drains before putting the cap back on?

options.A: To create the suction needed to pull out fluid
options.B: To clean the inside of the chamber
options.C: To keep the plastic from cracking
options.D: To push trapped air out through the drain site

explanation: Compressing the bulb and sealing it creates a vacuum that gently pulls fluid from the surgical site. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why is it important to pin or secure drainage tubing to the patient's clothing?

options.A: To help fluid flow upward
options.B: To keep the collection bag hidden
options.C: To stop the drain from being accidentally pulled out
options.D: To warm up the fluid inside

explanation: Securing the tube gives it some slack so moving around doesn't yank the drain out of the wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which action is dangerous if a surgical drain is accidentally pulled out partway?

options.A: Pushing the tubing back into the wound
options.B: Checking the patient's vital signs
options.C: Putting a sterile dressing over the opening
options.D: Calling the doctor

explanation: Pushing a slipped tube back inside carries skin germs straight into the sterile wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: A patient's suction drain stops working, and the area becomes tight and painful. What should you check first?

options.A: Turn the suction pressure all the way up
options.B: Remove the drain right away
options.C: Check the tubing for kinks or blood clots
options.D: Wash out the wound with tap water

explanation: Kinks and clots are the most common reasons a drain suddenly stops working. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: Why is a patient asked to hold their breath or bear down when a drain is being removed?

options.A: To stop air from entering the empty tract
options.B: To make urine flow faster
options.C: To numb the skin
options.D: To relax the stomach muscles

explanation: This breathing technique changes pressure in the body, lowering the risk of air getting into the tissue space. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What kind of dressing is usually put on right after a drain is taken out?

options.A: A sterile dressing that seals the wound
options.B: A tight plaster cast
options.C: Wet gauze soaked in sterile water
options.D: A loose elastic bandage

explanation: An airtight dressing covers the opening to stop fluid leaks and keep bacteria out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing bladder irrigation?

options.A: To measure accurate daily fluid intake levels
options.B: To stimulate normal kidney function and urine output
options.C: To maintain catheter patency and remove clots
options.D: To permanently cure chronic urinary tract infections

explanation: Irrigation flushes out debris and blood clots that could otherwise block urine flow through the catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h1)

question: Why is bladder irrigation frequently ordered following prostate surgery?

options.A: It speeds up the healing of abdominal skin incisions
options.B: Anesthetics permanently paralyze the urinary sphincter muscles
options.C: Surgical patients lose the ability to produce natural urine
options.D: Post-operative bleeding can form clots and block the catheter

explanation: Surgeries near the prostate often cause bleeding, making regular clearing necessary to prevent dangerous urinary retention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h1)

question: Which clinical condition is a clear indication for bladder irrigation?

options.A: Severe chronic kidney disease with low output
options.B: Mild dehydration in an elderly patient
options.C: An uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection
options.D: Presence of gross hematuria with clot formation

explanation: Blood clots pose a major risk of catheter blockage, making irrigation necessary to clear the pathway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h2)

question: Why is recent urinary tract trauma a contraindication for bladder irrigation?

options.A: It instantly causes permanent kidney failure in patients
options.B: Fluid pressure can worsen injuries and spread infection
options.C: The bladder muscle cannot hold any liquid volume
options.D: Sterile water reacts dangerously with exposed blood

explanation: Introducing fluid and pressure into a traumatized tract can tear fragile tissues and introduce bacteria deeper. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h2)

question: What is a major disadvantage of using an open bladder irrigation system?

options.A: It requires specialized triple-lumen catheters every time
options.B: Increased risk of introducing bacteria into the urinary tract
options.C: Patients experience much more severe abdominal pain
options.D: The procedure takes significantly longer to complete

explanation: Disconnecting the catheter junction exposes the sterile interior to airborne and contact contaminants. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h3)

question: Why do healthcare facilities prefer closed continuous bladder irrigation systems?

options.A: They cost less money than standard single-lumen catheters
options.B: Patients can easily manage the equipment at home alone
options.C: They completely eliminate the need for nurse monitoring
options.D: They maintain sterility by avoiding disconnection of tubing

explanation: Keeping the drainage system intact drastically lowers the chance of hospital-acquired urinary tract infections. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h3)

question: What type of fluid is most commonly used for bladder irrigation?

options.A: Concentrated antiseptic liquid
options.B: 5% Dextrose in water solution
options.C: Plain tap water from the sink
options.D: Sterile normal saline solution

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic and safe for internal mucosal contact without causing fluid shifts. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h4)

question: Why should the irrigation fluid be warmed to room temperature before use?

options.A: Warm water prevents the IV tubing from clogging
options.B: Cold fluid can trigger painful bladder spasms
options.C: Cold saline damages the internal catheter balloon
options.D: Warm fluid dissolves blood clots much faster

explanation: Introducing cold liquids directly into the bladder irritates the detrusor muscle, causing painful spasms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h4)

question: A patient on continuous bladder irrigation has an input of 2000 mL and a catheter drainage output of 1500 mL over eight hours. What is the nurse's immediate priority?

options.A: Administer a strong diuretic medication to stimulate urine
options.B: Check the tubing for kinks and assess for catheter blockage
options.C: Remove the urinary catheter immediately to relieve pressure
options.D: Document the findings and increase the irrigation flow rate

explanation: A negative fluid balance where output is less than input often signals a clot obstruction that requires immediate intervention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h5)

question: Which lumen of a triple-lumen catheter is attached to the continuous irrigation bag?

options.A: The balloon inflation port
options.B: The irrigation influx port
options.C: The medication injection port
options.D: The main urine drainage port

explanation: The dedicated irrigation channel delivers the sterile fluid directly into the bladder cavity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h5)

question: During manual intermittent irrigation, what action should the nurse take if resistance is felt while pushing the fluid?

options.A: Inject air into the syringe to push the clot through
options.B: Inflate the catheter balloon with extra sterile water
options.C: Apply more physical force to clear the blockage
options.D: Stop instilling immediately and report the resistance

explanation: Forcing fluid against resistance can rupture the bladder or damage delicate tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h6)

question: How is the irrigating fluid typically drained out during an intermittent procedure?

options.A: By clamping the drainage bag and waiting an hour
options.B: By using a heavy mechanical suction machine
options.C: By asking the patient to forcefully push it out
options.D: By lowering the catheter to allow gravity drainage

explanation: Gravity safely guides the instilled fluid and debris out of the bladder and into the collection container. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h6)

question: What is a common cause of painful bladder spasms in a patient undergoing continuous irrigation?

options.A: Too much oral water intake during the night
options.B: The presence of the balloon in the urethra
options.C: An allergic reaction to the drainage bag material
options.D: A blocked catheter or cold irrigation solution

explanation: Obstructions causing overdistention or cold fluid touching the bladder wall directly triggers spasms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h7)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take when drainage suddenly stops during continuous bladder irrigation?

options.A: Inspect the tubing for kinks, twists, or patient sitting on it
options.B: Immediately pull out the catheter to prevent infection
options.C: Instill 100 mL of ice-cold water to shock the bladder
options.D: Disconnect the drainage bag and leave the catheter open

explanation: Always rule out simple mechanical obstructions like a kinked tube before attempting invasive flushes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h7)

question: Which detail is essential to include in the nursing documentation after a bladder irrigation?

options.A: Net fluid balance and characteristics of the drainage
options.B: The cost of the sterile saline bottles used
options.C: The patient's personal religious preferences
options.D: The exact brand name of the IV pole used

explanation: Recording fluid balance and drainage appearance helps evaluate the effectiveness of the procedure and patient safety. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h8)

question: Why is calculating the net fluid balance crucial during continuous bladder irrigation?

options.A: To prove that the nurse completed the shift duties
options.B: To ensure the patient is not retaining excess irrigation fluid
options.C: To calculate the exact hospital bill for the patient
options.D: To determine when the patient can eat solid foods

explanation: Tracking input against output prevents fluid overload and confirms that the drainage system is unobstructed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of assisted feeding in clinical nursing practice?

options.A: To speed up the hospital discharge process for doctors
options.B: To prevent malnutrition and dehydration in vulnerable patients
options.C: To replace the need for intravenous fluid administration
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital food supplies

explanation: Assisted feeding directly targets nutritional deficits in patients unable to eat independently, safeguarding their physical health and recovery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: A newly admitted stroke patient is drowsy and struggles to clear secretions. What initial action should the nurse take?

options.A: Request total parenteral nutrition without performing an oral assessment
options.B: Assess swallowing ability and level of consciousness before offering food
options.C: Place a large-bore nasogastric tube right away without further checks
options.D: Feed the patient immediately with thin liquids to restore lost energy

explanation: Checking consciousness and swallow safety first prevents aspiration risks in vulnerable neurological patients. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why should bedside commodes and soiled items be removed before a meal?

options.A: To comply with hospital infection control laundry protocols
options.B: To prevent family members from complaining about the ward
options.C: To maintain a pleasant and appetizing environment for eating
options.D: To create extra space for the nurse to sit by the bed

explanation: A clean environment free of unpleasant sights and smells encourages better appetite and dignity during meals. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: Checking the diet tray against the patient's care plan primarily serves what purpose?

options.A: Verifying that the patient paid the correct hospital meal fees
options.B: Checking if the cutlery provided is clean and rust-free
options.C: Confirming that the hospital kitchen sent enough meat portions
options.D: Ensuring the served meal matches the prescribed medical diet

explanation: Verifying the diet prevents adverse clinical events like giving regular food to a patient ordered for a strict diabetic or renal diet. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: At what bed angle should a semi-conscious patient be positioned for oral feeding?

options.A: 15 to 30 degrees
options.B: 45 degrees prone
options.C: 60 to 90 degrees
options.D: Zero degrees flat

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed to a high Fowler's position utilizes gravity to direct food into the esophagus and away from the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the clinical rationale for keeping a patient upright after eating?

options.A: It improves blood circulation to the lower extremities
options.B: It helps the nurse clear away the food tray more quickly
options.C: It allows the digestive enzymes to work faster in the stomach
options.D: It prevents gastric reflux and subsequent pulmonary aspiration

explanation: Remaining upright for thirty minutes post-meal reduces the likelihood of food backing up into the pharynx and entering the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: How should the nurse offer food bites during assisted feeding?

options.A: Mixed together into a single paste
options.B: In small, manageable amounts
options.C: In large scoops to finish quickly
options.D: Only when the patient demands it

explanation: Small portions reduce the risk of choking and allow the patient to chew and swallow comfortably. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is it important to talk to an unresponsive patient while feeding them?

options.A: It helps speed up their neurological recovery process
options.B: It maintains dignity and prepares them for incoming food
options.C: It keeps the nurse awake during long night shifts
options.D: It proves to relatives that the nurse is doing work

explanation: Verbal communication respects the patient's personhood and provides a vital cue that eating is about to occur. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: What makes silent aspiration particularly dangerous in dysphagic patients?

options.A: It occurs without the protective reflex of coughing or choking
options.B: It only happens when nurses are absent from the ward
options.C: It cannot be detected by any medical diagnostic equipment
options.D: It causes immediate respiratory arrest within seconds

explanation: Because the patient does not cough, food enters the lungs unnoticed, often leading to undetected pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: A patient with moderate dementia wanders away from the dining table and refuses to eat. What nursing intervention is most effective?

options.A: Provide finger foods that the patient can eat while walking
options.B: Force the patient to sit down and feed them by physical restraint
options.C: Administer a sedative drug to calm the patient down for lunch
options.D: Withhold all meals until the patient asks for food willingly

explanation: Adapting to the patient's pacing and providing accessible finger foods helps maintain nutrition without triggering behavioral agitation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is a key post-feeding task to prevent oral infections in dependent patients?

options.A: Weighing the food tray on a kitchen scale
options.B: Performing oral hygiene and cleaning the mouth
options.C: Applying fresh dressings to the patient's bed
options.D: Giving the patient a strong sleeping pill

explanation: Removing leftover food particles from the oral cavity prevents bacterial growth, thrush, and aspiration of debris. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is accurate documentation of meal intake critical for hospitalized patients?

options.A: It is required for calculating the daily laundry budget
options.B: It allows the healthcare team to monitor nutritional adequacy
options.C: It helps patients check their own grocery bills later
options.D: It proves to the hospital management that nurses worked

explanation: Tracking food and fluid intake percentages helps identify nutritional deficits early and guides dietary adjustments. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of a gastrostomy feeding tube?

options.A: To deliver nutrition directly into the stomach
options.B: To decompress the liver during hepatic failure
options.C: To remove excess gas from the small intestine
options.D: To bypass a blockage in the large bowel

explanation: A gastrostomy tube creates a direct route into the stomach for delivering food, fluids, and medications when oral intake is impossible. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h1)

question: A patient with severe dysphagia from a stroke needs long-term nutritional support. Why is a gastrostomy preferred over a nasogastric tube?

options.A: It allows the patient to continue eating normally by mouth
options.B: It completely prevents the risk of aspiration pneumonia
options.C: It requires surgical removal after every single feeding session
options.D: It is intended for long-term use and reduces nasal mucosal irritation

explanation: Nasogastric tubes are prone to causing nasal tissue breakdown and are typically restricted to short-term use, whereas gastrostomies suit long-term nutritional needs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which gastrostomy tube sits flat against the skin and is often used for active patients?

options.A: Standard nasogastric catheter
options.B: Weighted feeding stylet
options.C: Open surgical jejunostomy
options.D: Low-profile button device

explanation: Button devices have a low profile that sits flush against the abdominal skin, offering comfort and discretion for mobile patients. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h2)

question: How does a PEG tube differ from a surgically placed open gastrostomy tube?

options.A: A PEG tube delivers food to the jejunum, while a surgical tube delivers food to the esophagus.
options.B: A PEG tube is made of solid metal, while surgical tubes are made of soft silicone.
options.C: A PEG tube is temporary and lasts only two days, while surgical tubes last for years.
options.D: A PEG tube is inserted using an endoscope and local anesthesia, whereas the other requires open abdominal surgery.

explanation: PEG insertion relies on endoscopic guidance through the abdominal wall, avoiding a traditional open surgical incision. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the minimum recommended bed elevation for a patient receiving a gastrostomy feeding?

options.A: 90 degrees upright
options.B: 30 to 45 degrees
options.C: Flat on the back
options.D: Trendelenburg position

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed reduces the risk of regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration during tube feeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: A nurse enters a patient's room to start a scheduled PEG feeding and finds the abdomen firm and tender with absent bowel sounds. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Proceed with the feeding at a slower pump rate
options.B: Lower the head of the bed to relieve abdominal pressure
options.C: Flush the tube vigorously with 100 mL of cold water
options.D: Hold the feeding and notify the prescribing clinician

explanation: Absent bowel sounds and a firm, tender abdomen suggest impaired GI motility or a potential complication, requiring the nurse to withhold the feed and report the finding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is water flushed through a gastrostomy tube before and after administering formula?

options.A: To stimulate rapid gastric emptying
options.B: To prevent tube clogging and maintain patency
options.C: To cool down warm enteral formula
options.D: To hydrate the liver and kidneys directly

explanation: Routine water flushes clear residual formula from the inner lumen, stopping the tube from blocking. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of checking gastric residual volume before a bolus feeding?

options.A: To determine the correct dosage of oral medications
options.B: To calculate the patient's daily fluid balance requirements
options.C: To measure the exact amount of gastric acid in the body
options.D: To gauge how well the stomach is emptying previous contents

explanation: Checking residuals helps nurses evaluate digestion and tolerance, preventing overfilling and subsequent aspiration. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which cleansing agent is generally recommended for routine daily cleaning of a gastrostomy stoma site?

options.A: Isopropyl rubbing alcohol
options.B: Povidone-iodine scrub solution
options.C: Mild soap and warm water
options.D: Full-strength hydrogen peroxide

explanation: Mild soap and water effectively clean the site without irritating the delicate peristomal skin or damaging healing tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why should nurses avoid tightening the external bolster too firmly against the abdominal wall?

options.A: It can cause pressure necrosis of the underlying skin
options.B: It increases the risk of accidental tube dislodgement
options.C: It will permanently seal the enteral feeding port
options.D: It causes the formula to digest too rapidly

explanation: Excessive pressure from a tight bolster restricts blood flow to the skin and gastric mucosa, leading to pressure ulcers or buried bumper syndrome. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h5)

question: What type of oral medication formulation should NOT be crushed for gastrostomy tube administration?

options.A: Basic chewable children's vitamins
options.B: Enteric-coated or sustained-release tablets
options.C: Standard uncoated scored tablets
options.D: Water-soluble powdered antibiotics

explanation: Crushing enteric-coated or sustained-release drugs destroys their specialized delivery mechanisms, potentially causing rapid drug toxicity or tube clogging. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why must different medications be flushed with water separately rather than mixed together in a single syringe?

options.A: To prevent drug-to-drug interactions and tube clogging
options.B: To ensure the total fluid volume remains under 10 mL
options.C: To speed up the hepatic first-pass metabolism process
options.D: To dilute the medication so it tastes better for the patient

explanation: Mixing crushed medications together can cause physical incompatibilities, creating a sludge that occludes the narrow tube lumen. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is the most immediate danger if a newly placed gastrostomy tube falls out?

options.A: The feeding pump will permanently explode
options.B: The patient will instantly develop severe hyperglycemia
options.C: The gastric acid will neutralize the abdominal wall
options.D: The stoma tract can close rapidly within hours

explanation: Because a new stoma has not formed a mature epithelial tract, it can narrow and close very quickly, making tube replacement difficult. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h7)

question: A patient with a PEG tube suddenly starts coughing and turning cyanotic during a continuous feeding. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Inject 50 mL of air to clear the gastric contents
options.B: Increase the pump rate to finish the formula faster
options.C: Stop the feeding immediately and assess the airway
options.D: Tighten the external bolster to stop formula leakage

explanation: Coughing and cyanosis during a feed strongly suggest aspiration, requiring an immediate stop to the feed and respiratory assessment. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h7)

question: Which sign should a nurse teach caregivers to report immediately as an indicator of stoma infection?

options.A: Normal bowel sounds heard during abdominal auscultation
options.B: Purulent drainage and spreading redness around the site
options.C: Mild skin discoloration directly under the soft bolster
options.D: Clear mucus discharge from the edges of the button

explanation: Purulent exudate and spreading erythema are classic signs of localized infection requiring medical evaluation and treatment. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h8)

question: Why is it important for family caregivers to have a spare replacement tube available at home?

options.A: To replace the feeding bag every time a new feed starts
options.B: To use as a measuring tool for daily abdominal girth
options.C: To connect two pumps together for simultaneous formulas
options.D: To prevent tract closure if the tube accidentally dislodges

explanation: Having a backup tube on hand allows rapid temporary insertion or preparation for clinical help, keeping the stoma tract from closing prematurely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h8)

question: What primary muscular movement propels food and waste through the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: Reflex action
options.B: Peristalsis
options.C: Aspiration
options.D: Osmosis

explanation: Peristalsis consists of coordinated wave-like muscle contractions that move contents forward through the digestive system. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary function of the colon during normal digestion and elimination?

options.A: Initiating the chemical digestion of dietary fats
options.B: Absorbing the majority of ingested food nutrients
options.C: Producing digestive enzymes for protein breakdown
options.D: Absorbing water and electrolytes from waste

explanation: The large intestine extracts water and minerals from indigestible food residue before excretion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h1)

question: A patient with a fecal impaction passes small amounts of liquid stool. What causes this symptom?

options.A: Complete paralysis of the internal anal sphincter muscle
options.B: Excessive oral fluid intake bypassing the stomach
options.C: Hyperactive peristalsis caused by a bacterial infection
options.D: Seepage of liquid feces around the hardened blockage

explanation: Liquid stool leaks past the impacted mass in the rectum, creating a false impression of diarrhea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which medication class is a well-known, frequent cause of chronic constipation in hospitalized patients?

options.A: Opioid analgesics
options.B: Loop diuretic drugs
options.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: Short-acting insulin

explanation: Opioids significantly slow gastrointestinal motility and reduce secretion, leading to hard, difficult-to-pass stools. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h2)

question: Why must a nurse auscultate bowel sounds before performing abdominal palpation?

options.A: Palpation can alter natural bowel motility and sounds
options.B: Deep touching immediately triggers a reflexive bowel movement
options.C: Auscultation warms up the abdominal wall muscles safely
options.D: Listening first prevents the patient from feeling nauseous

explanation: Pressing on the abdomen stimulates peristalsis, which would give a false reading of active bowel sounds. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h3)

question: What diagnostic procedure allows direct visualization of the entire large intestine lining?

options.A: Colonoscopy
options.B: Urinalysis
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound
options.D: Barium swallow

explanation: A colonoscopy uses a flexible camera tube inserted through the rectum to inspect the colon mucosa directly. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary rationale for encouraging early ambulation in a postoperative patient at risk for constipation?

options.A: Walking increases renal filtration of metabolic waste products
options.B: Physical movement stimulates normal gastrointestinal motility
options.C: Physical activity prevents abdominal wall muscle atrophy
options.D: Exercise directly softens hard stool inside the rectum

explanation: Physical activity activates skeletal and smooth muscle systems, helping restart sluggish bowel movements after surgery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h4)

question: What nursing action is essential when caring for a patient experiencing severe watery diarrhea?

options.A: Applying protective barrier cream to the perianal skin
options.B: Performing daily digital removal of fecal impactions
options.C: Administering bulk-forming laxatives to bulk up the stool
options.D: Restricting all oral fluid intake to rest the bowel

explanation: Frequent watery stool causes severe skin breakdown and irritation, making barrier protection a priority. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h4)

question: What instruction should a nurse give a patient who is starting a high-fiber diet to prevent constipation?

options.A: Take a strong stimulant laxative with every single meal
options.B: Restrict physical exercise until the digestive system adjusts
options.C: Eliminate all dairy products to reduce digestive gas
options.D: Increase daily fluid intake alongside the dietary changes

explanation: Fiber absorbs water in the gut; without adequate fluids, high fiber intake actually causes severe constipation and cramping. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which symptom is a critical red flag that requires immediate medical reporting in a patient with bowel issues?

options.A: Rectal bleeding
options.B: Mild morning flatulence
options.C: Minor abdominal rumbling
options.D: Temporary appetite loss

explanation: Rectal bleeding can indicate serious conditions like hemorrhoids, polyps, or colorectal malignancy requiring prompt investigation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the colon during normal digestion?

options.A: Producing digestive enzymes
options.B: Secreting bile for fat breakdown
options.C: Absorbing water and electrolytes
options.D: Filtering metabolic waste from blood

explanation: The main role of the large intestine is to absorb water and remaining electrolytes from waste material before excretion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why does prolonged stool transit time lead to hard stools?

options.A: The rectum walls lose elasticity
options.B: Mucus production stops completely
options.C: Bacterial fermentation increases rapidly
options.D: Excessive water is removed by the colon

explanation: Staying in the colon longer exposes the waste to continuous water absorption, drying out the stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h1)

question: A common medication class frequently responsible for causing secondary constipation is:

options.A: Opioid analgesics
options.B: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.C: Loop diuretics
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Opioids slow down bowel motility significantly by binding to receptors in the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: How does hypothyroidism contribute to the development of constipation?

options.A: Causing severe dehydration through excessive sweating
options.B: Slowing down overall metabolic and bowel activity
options.C: Weakening the abdominal wall muscles directly
options.D: Increasing the absorption of dietary fats

explanation: Low thyroid hormone levels reduce metabolic rate, which translates to sluggish peristalsis across the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which clinical tool is commonly used by nurses to classify stool consistency?

options.A: APGAR scoring system
options.B: Bristol Stool Chart
options.C: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.D: Braden Scale for Pressure Ulcers

explanation: The Bristol Stool Chart categorizes human stool into seven types based on shape and consistency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h3)

question: A patient reports lower abdominal fullness and straining without passing stool for four days. What is the immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Encourage the patient to walk for two hours straight
options.B: Perform a detailed bowel history and physical assessment
options.C: Insert a urinary catheter to relieve bladder pressure
options.D: Administer a strong oral stimulant laxative immediately

explanation: Assessment must precede any intervention to understand the exact nature and duration of the problem. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which laxative category works primarily by drawing water into the intestinal lumen?

options.A: Stimulant laxatives
options.B: Stool softeners
options.C: Bulk-forming agents
options.D: Osmotic laxatives

explanation: Osmotic agents create an osmotic gradient that pulls water into the colon to soften the stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why must patients taking bulk-forming laxatives increase their fluid intake significantly?

options.A: To prevent the supplement from causing bowel obstruction
options.B: To prevent severe electrolyte depletion from diarrhea
options.C: To activate the chemical properties of the medication
options.D: To speed up the absorption of the drug into the bloodstream

explanation: Bulk-forming agents require ample water to expand properly; without fluids, they can solidify and worsen blockages. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which physiological process is triggered shortly after eating and aids in stimulating bowel movements?

options.A: Baroreceptor response
options.B: Renal clearance rate
options.C: Hepatic portal shunt
options.D: Gastrocolic reflex

explanation: Ingesting food triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which increases motor activity in the colon. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of elevating a patient's feet with a stool while they are on the toilet?

options.A: It straightens the anorectal angle to ease stool passage
options.B: It prevents venous pooling in the lower extremities
options.C: It relaxes the internal anal sphincter automatically
options.D: It increases intra-abdominal pressure without using muscles

explanation: Raising the knees changes the posture from sitting to a squat-like position, aligning the rectum for easier evacuation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is a major complication of chronic, untreated constipation involving a hard mass trapped in the rectum?

options.A: Bowel perforation
options.B: Diverticulitis
options.C: Fecal impaction
options.D: Intestinal ischemia

explanation: Fecal impaction occurs when dry, hard stool packs the rectum so tightly that normal peristalsis cannot move it out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which symptom often indicates overflow diarrhea in a patient with a severe fecal impaction?

options.A: Sudden onset of projectile green vomiting
options.B: Seepage of liquid stool around the impacted mass
options.C: Passing large, formed stools multiple times a day
options.D: Complete cessation of all gastrointestinal sounds

explanation: Liquid stool from higher up in the colon leaks around the blockage, which can easily be mistaken for diarrhea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the minimum number of loose stools per day that defines diarrhoea?

options.A: Ten infrequent dry movements daily
options.B: Only one watery stool per day
options.C: Five hard stools every morning
options.D: Three or more loose stools daily

explanation: Diarrhoea is medically defined as passing three or more loose or liquid stools within a twenty-four-hour period. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h1)

question: A patient has been passing loose stools for 20 days. How is this classified?

options.A: Persistent diarrhoea
options.B: Chronic malabsorption
options.C: Normal infant pattern
options.D: Acute gastroenteritis

explanation: Any diarrhoeal episode lasting from 14 days up to a month is classified as persistent diarrhoea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which mechanism involves unabsorbable solutes drawing water into the bowel lumen?

options.A: Secretory diarrhoea
options.B: Osmotic diarrhoea
options.C: Exudative diarrhoea
options.D: Motility diarrhoea

explanation: Osmotic diarrhoea occurs when poorly absorbed substances remain in the gut and hold onto water through osmotic pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h2)

question: Bacterial toxins causing active ion secretion into the gut result in which type of diarrhoea?

options.A: Secretory diarrhoea
options.B: Exudative diarrhoea
options.C: Osmotic diarrhoea
options.D: Mechanical diarrhoea

explanation: Secretory mechanisms involve continuous fluid and electrolyte secretion driven by toxins, leading to large volumes of watery stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is a specific sign of dehydration unique to infants with severe diarrhoea?

options.A: Sunken fontanelles
options.B: Widened pulse pressure
options.C: Bulging eye sockets
options.D: Flushed dry skin

explanation: The soft spots on an infant's skull sink inward when total body fluid drops significantly due to fluid loss. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h3)

question: A patient with acute watery diarrhoea shows poor skin turgor and dry mucous membranes. What does this indicate?

options.A: Localized skin infection
options.B: Normal baseline hydration status
options.C: Extracellular fluid volume deficit
options.D: Primary electrolyte overload

explanation: Dry mucous membranes and slow skin recoil reflect systemic dehydration caused by ongoing fluid losses from the gut. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h3)

question: Which test is used to identify specific bacterial pathogens in stool?

options.A: Stool culture and sensitivity
options.B: Liver function test
options.C: Random blood glucose
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: Stool cultures grow and isolate specific bacteria so the laboratory can find out which antibiotics will treat the infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why is serum urea and creatinine measured in a patient with severe diarrhoea?

options.A: To screen for primary liver damage
options.B: To monitor kidney function affected by fluid loss
options.C: To measure direct parasite load in the blood
options.D: To determine the exact carbohydrate intake

explanation: Severe fluid loss reduces blood flow to the kidneys, causing urea and creatinine levels to rise in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why are drugs that slow bowel movement avoided in patients with invasive bacterial diarrhoea?

options.A: They trap pathogens in the gut and worsen toxicity
options.B: They neutralize oral rehydration solutions completely
options.C: They convert bacterial infections into viral ones
options.D: They instantly cause permanent renal failure

explanation: Slowing down the bowel prevents the body from passing out harmful bacteria and toxins, which prolongs the illness. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which supplement is recommended by the WHO to reduce duration and severity in young children with diarrhoea?

options.A: Vitamin C tablets
options.B: Iron drops
options.C: Zinc supplementation
options.D: Calcium carbonate

explanation: Zinc supports immune function in the gut and shortens the recovery period during diarrhoeal illnesses in children. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h5)

question: What biological mechanism makes oral rehydration salts effective?

options.A: Direct antimicrobial action against gut parasites
options.B: Active gastric acid inhibition in the stomach
options.C: Sodium-glucose cotransport in the small intestine
options.D: Passive water absorption through the large colon

explanation: Glucose helps actively move sodium across the intestinal lining, pulling water along with it into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h6)

question: A patient with severe dehydration from cholera is admitted to the ward. What is the immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Collect a 24-hour dietary intake diary
options.B: Administer heavy doses of oral antimotility drugs
options.C: Prepare the patient for immediate discharge
options.D: Initiate rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation

explanation: Severe dehydration affects blood circulation and requires urgent IV fluid replacement to stabilize the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h6)

question: What primary electrolyte loss during severe diarrhoea can lead to heart rhythm problems?

options.A: Potassium
options.B: Chloride
options.C: Calcium
options.D: Magnesium

explanation: Low blood potassium levels disrupt the electrical activity of heart muscle, which can lead to dangerous heart rhythms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why does metabolic acidosis commonly happen in patients with severe watery diarrhoea?

options.A: Increased production of gastric hydrochloric acid
options.B: Excessive loss of bicarbonate ions in the stool
options.C: Failure of the kidneys to filter dietary proteins
options.D: Rapid retention of carbon dioxide in the lungs

explanation: Intestinal fluids contain a lot of bicarbonate. Losing large amounts of stool drains these alkaline buffers, making the blood acidic. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is faecal incontinence defined as?

options.A: Frequent cramping before bowel movements
options.B: The inability to pass hard stools
options.C: The involuntary loss of stool or gas
options.D: Painful swelling of the anal sphincter

explanation: Faecal incontinence specifically refers to the lack of control resulting in the involuntary leakage of faecal material or gas. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why do many Nigerian patients delay seeking care for faecal incontinence?

options.A: Strict hospital admission criteria
options.B: Availability of cheap local herbal cures
options.C: Lack of trained nurses in primary clinics
options.D: Cultural stigma surrounding the condition

explanation: Social embarrassment and cultural stigma often prevent individuals from reporting bowel control issues early. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which muscle provides involuntary resting tone to the anus?

options.A: External anal sphincter
options.B: Puborectalis muscle
options.C: Internal anal sphincter
options.D: Levator ani muscle

explanation: The internal anal sphincter is composed of smooth muscle and functions involuntarily to keep the anus closed at rest. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the puborectalis muscle in bowel control?

options.A: Creating an acute angle to prevent stool leakage
options.B: Producing mucus for smooth stool passage
options.C: Pumping blood away from the anal cushions
options.D: Sensing the temperature of rectal contents

explanation: The puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction forward, creating a sharp angle that helps keep faeces in the rectum. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is a major obstetric cause of faecal incontinence in women?

options.A: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.B: Frequent urinary tract infections
options.C: Prolonged obstructed labour
options.D: High maternal blood pressure

explanation: Difficult labour and perineal tears during childbirth frequently damage the anal sphincter complex in women. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h3)

question: A patient with a recent stroke develops faecal incontinence. What is the primary cause?

options.A: Direct mechanical injury to the anal sphincter
options.B: Disruption of neural control over the bowel
options.C: Chronic inflammation of the rectal lining
options.D: Severe localized bacterial infection

explanation: Brain injuries like stroke interfere with the neurological pathways required for voluntary bowel control and sensation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h3)

question: What characterizes passive faecal incontinence?

options.A: Leakage occurs without any prior warning or urge
options.B: Stool escapes only when the patient coughs heavily
options.C: Watery stool leaks around a hard fecal mass
options.D: The patient feels an urgent need but cannot hold it

explanation: In passive incontinence, stool escapes unnoticed because the patient lacks sensation or has a persistently open sphincter. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h4)

question: A bedridden elderly patient leaks liquid stool around a hard impaction. What type of incontinence is this?

options.A: Neurogenic incontinence
options.B: Urge incontinence
options.C: Passive incontinence
options.D: Overflow incontinence

explanation: Liquid stool leaks past a blockage when faecal impaction prevents normal rectal emptying. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h4)

question: What physical assessment technique evaluates anal sphincter tone?

options.A: Inspection of the umbilicus
options.B: Digital rectal examination
options.C: Abdominal percussion
options.D: Auscultation of bowel sounds

explanation: A gloved, lubricated finger inserted into the rectum allows the nurse or doctor to feel resting and squeeze pressures of the sphincter. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which diagnostic test is best used to visualize structural tears in the anal sphincter?

options.A: Endoanal ultrasound
options.B: Plain abdominal radiograph
options.C: Barium swallow study
options.D: Routine urinalysis

explanation: Endoanal ultrasound provides detailed images of the internal and external sphincter layers to detect structural damage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of a bowel training program?

options.A: Completely eliminating the need for dietary fibre
options.B: Establishing a predictable routine for evacuation
options.C: Inducing permanent constipation in the patient
options.D: Preventing the consumption of any solid foods

explanation: Bowel training aims to help the patient empty the bowel at set times, reducing unpredictable leakage episodes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h6)

question: How does dietary soluble fibre assist in managing faecal incontinence?

options.A: By speeding up transit time to prevent digestion
options.B: By absorbing excess water to form a more solid stool
options.C: By relaxing the internal sphincter muscle completely
options.D: By killing bacteria that cause loose bowel movements

explanation: Soluble fibre adds bulk and consistency to liquid stools, making them easier to control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h6)

question: What product is commonly applied to protect perianal skin from stool?

options.A: Zinc oxide barrier ointment
options.B: Antiseptic surgical spirit
options.C: Alcohol-based rubbing liquid
options.D: Perfumed body lotion

explanation: Barrier creams containing zinc oxide create a protective layer shielding the skin from moisture and digestive enzymes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why should nurses pat the perianal skin dry instead of rubbing it?

options.A: To speed up the evaporation of moisture completely
options.B: To prevent friction injury to fragile, irritated skin
options.C: To stimulate local blood flow to the anal sphincter
options.D: To ensure the barrier cream dries instantly

explanation: Rubbing inflamed skin causes further mechanical trauma and worsens breakdown or dermatitis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h7)

question: What common psychological response is often seen in patients with faecal incontinence?

options.A: Social withdrawal and depression
options.B: Excessive excitement and talkativeness
options.C: Aggressive behavior toward staff
options.D: Denial of any physical symptoms

explanation: The embarrassment and loss of control associated with the condition frequently lead to isolation and depressive symptoms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h8)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates holistic support for a patient experiencing social isolation due to incontinence?

options.A: Advising the patient to stay indoors permanently
options.B: Discussing discreet management options and coping strategies openly
options.C: Focusing solely on medication administration without talking
options.D: Telling the patient that the condition is untreatable

explanation: Providing practical solutions like absorbent pads and reassurance helps restore confidence and encourages social re-engagement. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of introducing barium sulfate during a lower GI series?

options.A: It stimulates immediate peristalsis to empty the bowel.
options.B: It cleanses the mucosal lining of accumulated fecal matter.
options.C: It numbs the rectal sphincter to reduce cramping pain.
options.D: It acts as a radiopaque contrast medium to highlight the colon.

explanation: Barium sulfate absorbs X-rays effectively, creating a clear visual contrast of the internal walls of the large intestine on radiographic images. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h1)

question: When might a clinician choose a barium enema instead of a routine colonoscopy?

options.A: When visualization of mucosal polyps under 2mm is required
options.B: When direct tissue biopsy of a lesion is urgently needed
options.C: When the patient has an active bowel perforation risk
options.D: When evaluating long segments or incomplete colonoscopies

explanation: Barium studies are useful for viewing the entire length of the large bowel, particularly when an endoscope cannot pass through an obstruction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h1)

question: The main finding associated with diverticular disease on a barium enema is...

options.A: diffuse shortening of the colon length
options.B: abnormal widening of the ileocecal valve
options.C: outpocketings of the colonic mucosa
options.D: complete absence of the rectal vault

explanation: Diverticular disease causes small pouches, or diverticula, to form along the wall of the colon, which fill with barium during the procedure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which condition is an absolute contraindication for performing a barium enema due to high mortality risk?

options.A: Suspected or known bowel perforation
options.B: Controlled essential hypertension
options.C: Mild chronic iron deficiency anemia
options.D: History of uncomplicated internal hemorrhoids

explanation: Leaking barium into the sterile peritoneal cavity causes severe chemical peritonitis and is a dangerous medical emergency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h3)

question: Why is a recent deep mucosal biopsy considered a risk factor for a barium enema?

options.A: The fresh tissue site may rupture under infusion pressure.
options.B: The biopsy site will completely neutralize the barium contrast.
options.C: Barium will instantly stain the biopsy site permanently black.
options.D: Enema fluid causes immediate local infection at the site.

explanation: Pressure from liquid and air can break open a recently compromised or surgically altered bowel wall, leading to leakage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h3)

question: Before scheduling a barium enema for a female patient of childbearing age, what must the nurse check?

options.A: Blood pressure baseline
options.B: Blood glucose level
options.C: Recent dental fillings
options.D: Pregnancy status

explanation: Ionizing radiation used during fluoroscopy poses significant risks to a developing fetus, making pregnancy verification mandatory. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why must the nurse inform the patient about the strong urge to defecate during the test?

options.A: To help the patient mentally prepare and hold the contrast in
options.B: To ensure the patient drinks extra water before the enema
options.C: To instruct the patient to immediately use the room restroom
options.D: To prompt the patient to request immediate pain relief drugs

explanation: Knowing that cramping and the urge to void are normal sensations helps patients cooperate and maintain the contrast enema without premature expulsion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why is a strict bowel cleansing protocol required before a barium enema?

options.A: Laxatives prevent severe cramping during the actual procedure.
options.B: Barium will not enter the rectum if stool is present inside.
options.C: Clear bowels speed up the elimination of the barium afterward.
options.D: Fecal residue can mimic polyps and obscure diagnostic findings.

explanation: Stool left in the colon creates shadows on the X-ray that radiologists can easily mistake for tumors or polyps. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h5)

question: A frail elderly patient is prescribed a rigorous bowel preparation. What is a primary nursing concern?

options.A: Sudden weight gain from fluid retention
options.B: Permanent loss of bowel control reflexes
options.C: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
options.D: Immediate development of a bowel blockage

explanation: Aggressive purgatives and clear liquid diets can quickly compromise vulnerable patients, leading to dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h5)

question: A patient becomes pale and dizzy with sweating during the barium infusion. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Immediate absorption of toxic barium into the bloodstream
options.B: Acute kidney failure triggered by the contrast fluid
options.C: An allergic reaction to the latex gloves used by staff
options.D: A vasovagal reaction from colonic distension and cramping

explanation: Stretching of the bowel wall can stimulate the vagus nerve, causing sudden drops in blood pressure and heart rate accompanied by diaphoresis and dizziness. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h6)

question: Why are frequent positional changes required during an air-contrast barium enema?

options.A: To evenly coat the colonic mucosal walls with the contrast medium
options.B: To help the patient expel the barium faster during the test
options.C: To prevent the rectal tip from falling out of position
options.D: To reduce the physical pressure on the lower lumbar spine

explanation: Moving the patient into different tilts ensures that both liquid barium and air spread uniformly across every section of the intestinal lining for better visualization. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a normal expected finding that the nurse should explain to the patient after a barium enema?

options.A: Rectal bleeding will occur for at least twenty-four hours.
options.B: Urine will turn dark brown due to systemic barium excretion.
options.C: Skin color will temporarily turn yellow from contrast absorption.
options.D: Stools will appear chalky white or light gray for a few days.

explanation: As the body clears the ingested or infused barium sulfate, bowel movements naturally take on a pale, chalky appearance. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h7)

question: What primary complication do post-procedure laxatives and high fluid intake help prevent?

options.A: Bacterial infection of the large intestine
options.B: Chronic malabsorption of dietary fats
options.C: Barium impaction and bowel obstruction
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the rectal sphincter

explanation: Barium solidifies as water is absorbed in the colon; fluids and laxatives keep the mixture moving to prevent a dangerous blockage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h7)
