options.C: It counts red blood cells in the sample droplet
options.D: It detects the temperature of the blood drop

explanation: The meter reads the physical changes resulting from the enzyme reaction and translates that data into a digital blood glucose value. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h2)

question: What should the nurse check on the test strip container before starting the procedure?

options.A: Container color
options.B: Manufacturer name
options.C: Country of origin
options.D: Expiration date

explanation: Using expired test strips can compromise the chemical reagents and produce inaccurate blood glucose readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why is warming a patient's cold hand recommended before performing a capillary blood draw?

options.A: It sterilizes the skin surface naturally
options.B: It improves blood flow and prevents painful squeezing
options.C: It numbs the fingertip to eliminate all pain
options.D: It activates the enzymes in the test strip

explanation: Warming increases peripheral circulation so a natural drop of blood forms easily without harsh milking that dilutes the sample with tissue fluid. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why must the nurse wipe away the very first drop of blood during capillary sampling?

options.A: It carries too many white blood cells
options.B: It contains tissue fluid that dilutes the sample
options.C: It causes the digital meter to display an error code
options.D: It is contaminated with external skin bacteria

explanation: The initial drop often contains serous fluid from the puncture that alters the glucose concentration, so the second drop is more reliable. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: What happens if a patient's skin is still wet with alcohol when the finger is pricked?

options.A: It prevents the lancing device from puncturing the skin
options.B: It causes severe bruising around the puncture site
options.C: It can alter the chemical reaction and test results
options.D: It permanently damages the digital screen of the meter

explanation: Residual alcohol mixes with the blood sample, leading to false high or low readings due to chemical interference. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the typical normal fasting blood glucose range for a healthy adult?

options.A: 70 to 99 mg/dL
options.B: 200 to 250 mg/dL
options.C: 40 to 60 mg/dL
options.D: 120 to 160 mg/dL

explanation: A fasting blood sugar between 70 and 99 mg/dL falls within the standard normal physiological range for non-diabetic adults. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: How should a nurse classify a random capillary blood glucose reading of 55 mg/dL in a conscious patient?

options.A: Hypoglycemia
options.B: Mild hyperglycemia
options.C: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.D: Normal fasting level

explanation: Any blood glucose value falling below 70 mg/dL is categorized as hypoglycemia and requires prompt corrective action. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: When is a quality control test using control solution necessary for a glucometer?

options.A: When opening a new vial of test strips
options.B: Before every single patient blood test
options.C: Once every three years during routine servicing
options.D: Only when the battery indicator light flashes red

explanation: Running control solution checks ensures that new strips and the meter are functioning correctly together. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why must test strips be stored in their original container with the lid tightly closed?

options.A: To protect the chemical reagents from environmental moisture
options.B: To keep the electronic chips inside the strips warm
options.C: To prevent the expiration date from fading away
options.D: To stop the strips from changing their physical color

explanation: Humidity damages the sensitive enzymes on test strips, leading to false or erratic glucose readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is a common cause of an unexpectedly high blood glucose reading after a patient eats?

options.A: Low room temperature affecting the meter screen
options.B: Using a lancet that is too small for the finger
options.C: Excessive pressure applied during blood collection
options.D: Food residue remaining on the patient's skin

explanation: Sugar from food or drink on unwashed fingers can falsely elevate capillary blood glucose readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: What should the nurse do first when a glucometer displays an error code on the screen?

options.A: Record the error code as a normal patient reading
options.B: Check the battery status and clean the strip port
options.C: Discard the entire glucometer device immediately
options.D: Administer emergency insulin based on the last reading

explanation: Most error codes are caused by power issues or dirt inside the testing chamber, which are easily fixed by maintenance steps. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why should lancing devices never be shared between different patients in a hospital?

options.A: The plastic casing will melt during chemical disinfection
options.B: Shared devices automatically drain the battery faster
options.C: Blood can backflow into the internal mechanical parts
options.D: Different patients require different color lancets

explanation: Internal parts of reusable lancing devices can trap microscopic blood droplets, transmitting pathogens if used on multiple people. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: Which infection control practice is NOT appropriate when performing bedside blood glucose testing?

options.A: Reusing a multi-patient lancing device if the needle is changed
options.B: Wearing clean non-sterile gloves during the sampling procedure
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before putting on and after removing gloves
options.D: Disposing of used lancets in a puncture-resistant sharps box

explanation: Multi-patient lancing devices pose a cross-infection risk and must be avoided in healthcare settings even with a new needle. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: What does a pulse oximeter measure?

options.A: Venous carbon dioxide
options.B: Total hemoglobin
options.C: Serum bicarbonate
options.D: Arterial oxygen saturation

explanation: Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites in the blood carrying oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h1)

question: Why does a pulse oximeter focus on pulsating blood flow?

options.A: To prevent the probe from overheating
options.B: To calculate the exact breathing rate
options.C: To ignore static light absorption from skin, bone, and venous blood
options.D: To measure total cardiac output per minute

explanation: Focusing on the pulse ensures the reading reflects arterial blood rather than surrounding tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h1)

question: What two types of light do standard pulse oximeter probes use?

options.A: X-ray and gamma radiation
options.B: Blue and yellow light
options.C: Ultraviolet and green light
options.D: Red and infrared light

explanation: Oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently, allowing the device to calculate saturation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the job of the photodetector in a pulse oximeter probe?

options.A: Warming up the skin to improve blood flow
options.B: Converting screen displays into beeps
options.C: Measuring the light that passes through the tissue
options.D: Generating the light needed for the test

explanation: The photodetector catches the unabsorbed light passing through the finger and sends that data to the machine's processor. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h2)

question: Why use a pulse oximeter for a patient with severe malaria and sudden trouble breathing?

options.A: To diagnose bacterial infections
options.B: To replace the need to count breaths
options.C: To measure the malaria parasite count
options.D: To catch low oxygen levels before blue skin discoloration appears

explanation: Pulse oximetry detects low oxygen early, long before physical signs like cyanosis show up. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which of these conditions does NOT require routine pulse oximetry monitoring?

options.A: Postoperative surgical recovery
options.B: Uncomplicated routine skin rash
options.C: Severe childhood pneumonia
options.D: Postpartum hemorrhage management

explanation: A simple skin rash does not affect breathing or oxygen levels, so oximetry is not needed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why should dark nail polish be removed before putting on a pulse oximeter sensor?

options.A: It blocks the device from turning on
options.B: It stains the plastic housing
options.C: It causes an allergic skin reaction
options.D: It absorbs the light and alters the reading

explanation: Dark nail polish blocks the light waves, causing falsely low oxygen readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h4)

question: What should a nurse do first if a patient's fingers are cold and pale during a check?

options.A: Tape the probe down tightly
options.B: Assume the patient is hypoxic and give oxygen
options.C: Gently warm the hand to improve blood flow
options.D: Switch immediately to an arterial blood gas draw

explanation: Cold fingers reduce blood flow and weaken the sensor signal. Warming the hand helps get an accurate reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is a major risk of raising oxygen to 100% in a patient with chronic lung disease?

options.A: Causing sudden permanent blindness
options.B: Destroying capillary beds
options.C: Triggering severe high blood pressure
options.D: Suppressing their drive to breathe and worsening carbon dioxide retention

explanation: Some chronic lung patients rely on low oxygen levels to stimulate breathing. Too much oxygen can make them stop breathing well. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h5)

question: An adult breathing room air has an SpO2 of 88%. How is this classified?

options.A: Mild hyperoxemia
options.B: Normal adult baseline
options.C: Significant hypoxia requiring action
options.D: An expected reading for healthy individuals

explanation: Any oxygen saturation below 90% is low and needs prompt medical attention. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h5)

question: How does severe shivering affect a pulse oximeter reading?

options.A: It pushes all blood out of the capillaries
options.B: It damages the infrared diodes inside
options.C: It turns off the battery
options.D: It creates movement noise that confuses the machine

explanation: Physical shaking makes it hard for the sensor to tell the difference between real pulse beats and movement. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h6)

question: Which environmental factor can cause false pulse oximeter readings?

options.A: Bright room light shining on the sensor
options.B: Strong electrical currents in wall sockets
options.C: Low air pressure at high altitudes
options.D: High room humidity

explanation: External light can leak into the sensor and interfere with the measurement. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h6)

question: A sensor has been taped to an unconscious patient's finger for over six hours. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Wrap gauze over it so it stays put
options.B: Remove the probe, check the skin, and move it to a new spot
options.C: Turn up the alarm volume
options.D: Leave it as long as the numbers look stable

explanation: Leaving a sensor in one spot too long can cause pressure sores. Nurses should rotate the site regularly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why is setting individual monitor alarms important for patient care?

options.A: It stops patients from pressing buttons
options.B: It prevents alarm fatigue so real drops in oxygen are not ignored
options.C: It saves battery power
options.D: It keeps the equipment warranty valid

explanation: Customizing alarms stops constant false ringing, which helps staff stay alert to real emergencies. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the main difference between a smart bed and a traditional hospital bed?

options.A: Smart beds use motorized mechanisms and digital sensors.
options.B: Smart beds require manual cranking for all position changes.
options.C: Traditional beds feature automated patient weight monitoring.
options.D: Traditional beds have built-in electronic health records.

explanation: Smart beds rely on automated motors and integrated sensors to carry out functions that traditionally required manual effort. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which hospital unit benefits the most from the advanced monitoring features of smart beds?

options.A: Intensive care units
options.B: General administrative offices
options.C: Outpatient eye clinics
options.D: Routine vaccination centers

explanation: Units caring for critically ill patients rely heavily on smart beds for continuous monitoring and rapid positioning adjustments. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which component of a smart bed lifts and tilts the mattress platform?

options.A: Infrared beams
options.B: Load cell sensors
options.C: Electric actuators
options.D: Pressure mapping mats

explanation: Actuators provide the mechanical power needed to adjust the height and angle of different bed sections. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h2)

question: How do exit-detection systems usually alert nurses that a patient is getting out of bed?

options.A: By using load cells or beams to trigger an alarm
options.B: By automatically locking all the wheels on the frame
options.C: By inflating the mattress side bolsters rapidly
options.D: By sending a text message to the hospital kitchen

explanation: Load cells and infrared sensors detect changes in weight distribution or movement, instantly alerting staff to potential falls. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h2)

question: Which patient is the best candidate for an automated bed exit alarm?

options.A: Experiencing mild dehydration on oral fluids
options.B: Recovering from a stable wrist fracture
options.C: At high risk for falls due to confusion
options.D: Scheduled for a minor skin biopsy

explanation: Patients who are confused or unsteady are prime candidates for exit alarms to prevent unassisted, dangerous attempts to get up. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h3)

question: Why are bariatric smart beds particularly helpful for nursing staff?

options.A: They reduce physical strain during patient repositioning.
options.B: They allow patients to walk unassisted much faster.
options.C: They eliminate the need for any nursing documentation.
options.D: They completely cure chronic underlying obesity.

explanation: Automated functions on heavy-duty beds spare nurses from heavy manual lifting and reduce workplace musculoskeletal injuries. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of continuous lateral rotation therapy in a smart bed?

options.A: To speed up the digestion of tube feedings
options.B: To make it easier to change bed linens completely
options.C: To redistribute pressure and prevent tissue breakdown
options.D: To measure the exact height of the patient daily

explanation: Continuous lateral rotation gently turns the patient to relieve prolonged pressure on bony prominences, protecting skin integrity. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h4)

question: How do smart bed scales improve accuracy when weighing vulnerable patients?

options.A: They calculate weight using only the angle of the head board.
options.B: They weigh the patient directly on the mattress without transfers.
options.C: They estimate weight based strictly on the patient's height.
options.D: They require the nurse to lift the patient off the bed first.

explanation: Weighing integrated into the bed frame allows precise measurements without disturbing critically ill or unstable patients. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h4)

question: What must a nurse check before turning on the automated turning features of a smart bed?

options.A: That tubing and cords have enough slack
options.B: That visitor chairs are pushed far away
options.C: That the patient has eaten a full meal
options.D: That the primary room windows are open

explanation: Ensuring lines like IV tubing or urinary catheters have slack prevents accidental pulling or dislodgement during bed movement. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why is regular testing of the bed backup battery important in clinical practice?

options.A: To calibrate the built-in nurse call system volume
options.B: To ensure positioning controls work during power failures
options.C: To prevent the mattress from becoming too warm
options.D: To stop the bed from moving around the room

explanation: Emergency backup power guarantees that essential adjustments and alarms remain functional when electricity fails. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take if a smart bed control panel stops working?

options.A: Call the hospital administrative director
options.B: Check the power source and connection plugs
options.C: Transfer the patient to a stretcher immediately
options.D: Disassemble the entire mattress mechanism

explanation: Simple power checks resolve many basic electronic failures before involving specialized technical repair teams. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why is special care required when cleaning the electronic components of a smart bed?

options.A: To prevent liquid from damaging internal sensors and wiring
options.B: To stop the cleaning chemicals from smelling too strong
options.C: To make the outer frame dry within five minutes
options.D: To ensure the bed changes color when washed properly

explanation: Moisture seeping into electronic seals can ruin actuators, sensors, and control systems, rendering the smart bed useless. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of healthcare simulation in nursing education?

options.A: To bridge classroom theory and clinical practice safely
options.B: To test student speed during emergency procedures
options.C: To reduce the number of qualified nursing instructors
options.D: To replace clinical placements entirely

explanation: Simulation provides a controlled environment allowing students to apply theoretical knowledge to practice without risking patient safety. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why is simulation particularly useful for large cohorts of nursing students?

options.A: It is much cheaper than maintaining standard hospital wards
options.B: It eliminates the need for any hospital-based training
options.C: It removes the need for formal student assessments
options.D: It guarantees every student hands-on procedural exposure

explanation: Crowded clinical wards can limit direct student participation, making simulation a reliable way to ensure all learners practice key skills. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h1)

question: Which simulator type is best suited for practicing an isolated skill like catheter insertion?

options.A: High-fidelity computerized manikin
options.B: Standardized patient actor
options.C: Virtual reality headset
options.D: Low-fidelity task trainer

explanation: Low-fidelity task trainers are specifically designed for practicing isolated technical procedures repeatedly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h2)

question: What distinguishes a high-fidelity simulator from a low-fidelity simulator?

options.A: Low-fidelity models breathe and bleed like real humans
options.B: High-fidelity models are only used for communication training
options.C: Low-fidelity models require complex computer programming
options.D: High-fidelity models respond physiologically to clinical interventions

explanation: High-fidelity manikins offer advanced physiological responses, changing vital signs based on student actions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h2)

question: What is the main goal of the pre-briefing stage in a simulation session?

options.A: To punish students who fail to read their textbooks
options.B: To clean and store the manikins after a session
options.C: To grade student performance on clinical speed
options.D: To establish psychological safety and outline learning objectives

explanation: Pre-briefing prepares students mentally, outlines expectations, and builds a safe environment for active learning. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h3)

question: What does the 'fiction contract' require from nursing students during a scenario?

options.A: To document fictional patient charts after clinical hours
options.B: To memorize a script written by the simulation instructor
options.C: To act as standardized patients for junior colleagues
options.D: To pretend the artificial scenario is a real clinical situation

explanation: The fiction contract asks learners to commit to the reality of the simulation while knowing they are in a safe learning space. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is considered the most critical phase of the simulation learning experience?

options.A: The post-scenario debriefing
options.B: The equipment setup phase
options.C: The active scenario execution
options.D: The pre-briefing orientation

explanation: Debriefing allows learners to reflect deeply on their clinical actions and construct new mental models for future practice. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h4)

question: Why is self-reflection encouraged during the debriefing session rather than a direct lecture from the instructor?

options.A: It prevents instructors from having to watch the simulation scenario
options.B: It saves time so the laboratory session can end much earlier
options.C: It ensures students never make a clinical mistake again
options.D: It helps students internalize lessons and critique their own clinical reasoning

explanation: Guided self-reflection promotes deeper critical thinking and long-term retention compared to simply being told what went wrong. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h4)

question: How does simulation directly contribute to improved patient safety?

options.A: By ensuring all student nurses work night shifts independently
options.B: By eliminating the need for pharmacology and pathology exams
options.C: By allowing students to practice high-risk skills without harming real patients
options.D: By replacing all bedside clinical supervision in teaching hospitals

explanation: Simulation provides a safe space to make and correct errors, protecting real patients from inexperienced hands. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h5)

question: A student nurse frequently freezes during rapid patient deterioration in the ward. What simulation benefit addresses this challenge?

options.A: Practicing crisis resource management and emergency scenarios repeatedly
options.B: Reading historical case studies about nursing pioneers
options.C: Memorizing textbook pharmacology tables during lecture hours
options.D: Observing senior nurses administer medications from afar

explanation: Simulated emergency scenarios build muscle memory and psychological readiness to handle rapid patient deterioration effectively. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h5)

question: What is a major financial barrier to implementing high-fidelity simulation in nursing schools?

options.A: Excessive student tuition fee refunds
options.B: Expensive uniforms required for simulation instructors
options.C: Mandatory daily travel costs for manikin repairs
options.D: High costs of purchasing, maintaining, and powering equipment

explanation: High-fidelity simulation requires heavy financial investment for equipment acquisition, maintenance, and reliable power. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h6)

question: Why is specialized faculty training necessary for effective simulation programs?

options.A: Instructors must learn how to repair computer motherboards
options.B: Facilitating a simulation requires different skills than traditional lecturing
options.C: Lecturers need to act as standardized patients during classes
options.D: Nursing councils forbid untrained teachers from grading exams

explanation: Running scenarios and leading debriefing sessions requires specific facilitation techniques distinct from standard classroom teaching. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary digital equivalent of a patient's traditional paper chart called?

options.A: Patient Billing Database
options.B: National Health Registry
options.C: Digital Pharmacy Archive
options.D: Electronic Medical Record

explanation: An Electronic Medical Record serves as the direct digital replacement for standard paper clinical charts. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h1)

question: How do EMRs primarily improve upon traditional paper-based health record systems in busy clinics?

options.A: By offering faster data retrieval and less physical storage
options.B: By automatically diagnosing complex patient diseases without testing
options.C: By completely eliminating the need for any clinical documentation
options.D: By removing all requirements for patient data privacy protection

explanation: Digital records clear up physical filing space while allowing instant access to patient histories. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h1)

question: Which EMR component alerts clinicians to potential drug allergies during prescription entry?

options.A: Clinical decision support
options.B: Inventory supply tracker
options.C: Physical storage module
options.D: Patient billing ledger

explanation: Clinical decision support tools warn staff about safety issues like allergies or dangerous drug interactions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of an audit trail inside an EMR system?

options.A: Ordering new medical supplies automatically
options.B: Calculating monthly hospital utility bills
options.C: Tracking who accessed or edited patient files
options.D: Scheduling nurse shift rotations

explanation: Audit trails record every interaction with a file to maintain security and accountability. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h2)

question: What common nursing documentation problem is instantly solved by switching to typed EMR entries?

options.A: Excessive use of medical supplies
options.B: Poor handwriting legibility
options.C: Delayed physician ward rounds
options.D: Inaccurate patient vital signs

explanation: Typed entries remove ambiguities caused by messy handwriting, reducing clinical errors. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h3)

question: A nurse uses barcode scanning on a patient wristband before drug administration to achieve what goal?

options.A: Updating the hospital staff attendance register
options.B: Recording daily ward temperature and humidity
options.C: Confirming the correct patient and medication match
options.D: Submitting the patient bill directly to the pharmacy

explanation: Barcode scanning verifies identity and prescription details right at the bedside to prevent administration errors. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h3)

question: Which infrastructure issue frequently threatens EMR usability in many Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: Excessive speed of internet routers
options.B: Lack of patient admission forms
options.C: Unstable electrical power supply
options.D: Too many available computer monitors

explanation: Frequent power outages interrupt digital record access, requiring reliable backup generators. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h4)

question: Why does unexpected EMR system downtime create clinical risks for nursing staff?

options.A: It prevents nurses from administering any oral medications
options.B: It forces a temporary return to paper records, risking documentation gaps
options.C: It deletes all historical patient records permanently
options.D: It automatically discharges all stable patients from the ward

explanation: Downtime disrupts normal workflow and can lead to missing or delayed documentation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h4)

question: What security practice ensures staff only view patient records relevant to their assigned duties?

options.A: Open ward notice boards
options.B: Public terminal placement
options.C: Shared departmental passwords
options.D: Role-based access control

explanation: Role-based access restricts file viewing to ensure staff only access data needed for their work. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h5)

question: Why is sharing personal EMR login credentials with a colleague a dangerous practice?

options.A: It compromises accountability and violates patient data confidentiality
options.B: It automatically shuts down the main hospital computer network
options.C: It doubles the internet data usage charges for the ward
options.D: It deletes all previous nursing entries in the system

explanation: Shared logins break audit trails and expose private health records to unauthorized eyes. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T9#GNS212_U4_T9_h5)

question: How do legal systems view digital EMR documentation compared to paper charting?

options.A: As unofficial notes with no legal importance

options.D: As temporary drafts that expire after one week

question: What is the correct action when a nurse forgets to document a care intervention and must add it later?

question: What primary ion is required for actin and myosin filaments to slide during muscle contraction?

options.A: Magnesium
options.B: Potassium
options.C: Sodium
options.D: Calcium

question: An intact neuromuscular pathway is necessary for skeletal muscle to achieve which outcome?

options.A: Uncontrolled spasm and twitching
options.B: Normal contraction and movement
options.C: Rapid bone mineralization
options.D: Increased blood cell production

question: The primary cause of muscle atrophy during prolonged bed rest is...

options.A: Rapid multiplication of red blood cells

options.D: Excessive calcium deposition in muscle tissue

explanation: Disuse reduces the metabolic demand for muscle proteins, shifting the cellular balance toward degradation rather than building. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h2)

question: A contracture develops in an immobile joint primarily because of what physiological change?

options.A: Complete destruction of the adjacent bone cortex
options.B: Replacement of muscle fibers with connective tissue
options.C: Massive accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule
options.D: Sudden elongation of the tendon sheath

explanation: Fibrous connective tissue and collagen shorten around the unused joint, permanently restricting normal movement. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h2)

question: A patient who can move a joint against gravity alone but cannot overcome any resistance has a muscle strength grade of...

options.A: Grade 1
options.B: Grade 4
options.C: Grade 3
options.D: Grade 5

explanation: Grade 3 denotes the ability to move the limb against the downward pull of gravity without any added resistance from the examiner. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h3)

question: What does a nurse eliminate when testing a patient with a muscle strength grade of two?

options.A: The effect of gravity on the limb
options.B: All nerve impulses from the spinal cord
options.C: The need for verbal instructions
options.D: The friction of the bed sheet

explanation: Placing the limb in a horizontal plane removes gravity, allowing weak muscles to show visible movement. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h3)

question: During passive range of motion exercises, the nurse should support the limb in what manner?

options.A: Above and below the joint
options.B: Directly over the joint capsule
options.C: Only at the proximal insertion point
options.D: Only at the distal fingertips

explanation: Supporting both sides of the joint protects vulnerable ligaments and ensures smooth, controlled movement. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why must a nurse stop passive range of motion exercises when meeting sudden firm resistance?

options.A: To test the patient for nerve damage
options.B: To allow the muscle time to produce calcium
options.C: To prevent injury to joint structures
options.D: To increase resting blood pressure

explanation: Forcing a joint past its current barrier of resistance can tear muscle fibers, tendons, and joint capsules. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h4)

question: The primary dietary component required for muscle protein synthesis and repair is...

options.A: Simple sugars
options.B: Complex starches
options.C: Saturated fats
options.D: Protein

explanation: Proteins break down into amino acids, which serve as the essential building blocks for repairing and maintaining muscle mass. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why is nutritional support critical for a patient experiencing prolonged muscular immobility?

options.A: It stops all electrical activity in the peripheral nerves
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for physical therapy
options.C: It reverses bone fractures within twenty-four hours
options.D: It counters the natural catabolic breakdown of muscle tissue

explanation: Inactivity shifts the body into a catabolic state, making sufficient nutrient intake necessary to slow muscle wasting. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h5)

question: What nursing intervention helps prevent foot drop in a bedridden patient?

options.A: Applying warm compresses to the toes
options.B: Elevating the head of the bed high
options.C: Massaging the calf muscles daily
options.D: Using a supportive footboard

explanation: A footboard keeps the feet in a neutral dorsiflexed position, preventing shortening of the Achilles tendon. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h6)

question: How often should a bedridden patient be repositioned to prevent skin breakdown and muscle strain?

options.A: Every six hours
options.B: Only when requested
options.C: Every two hours
options.D: Once every shift

explanation: Regular turning every two hours relieves sustained pressure on bony prominences and maintains circulation to compressed tissues. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is another name for gallows traction?

options.A: Russell's traction
options.B: Buck's extension
options.C: Bryant's traction
options.D: Balanced skeletal traction

explanation: Bryant's traction is another name for gallows traction. It is named after the surgeon who introduced this vertical suspension method for treating femur fractures in young children. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is gallows traction only used for infants under two years old?

options.A: Bone healing in older toddlers occurs too rapidly for skin traction.
options.B: Older children refuse to stay quiet in a vertical suspension.
options.C: Heavier children can pull the bed over and ruin the traction setup.
options.D: Infant skin is too fragile for any other type of heavy bandage.

explanation: Children weighing over 14 kg are too heavy for this setup. Their weight can destabilize the frame, making the traction unsafe and ineffective. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h1)

question: Is gallows traction appropriate for a three-year-old child with a broken femur?

options.A: Yes, if nursing staff provide continuous physical restraint.
options.B: No, because toddlers only receive skeletal pin traction.
options.C: Yes, provided the frame is secured to the wall.
options.D: No, because the child is too old and heavy for it.

explanation: Children over two years old or above 14 kg exceed the safe weight and age limits for gallows traction, so other methods must be used. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h2)

question: Gallows traction is most commonly used to treat a fracture of the:

options.A: Clavicle
options.B: Tibia
options.C: Femur
options.D: Humerus

explanation: Gallows traction lifts and aligns the legs to treat broken thigh bones (femur fractures) in infants. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h2)

question: How should the traction weights be positioned during your routine checks?

options.A: Supported on a small stool placed beside the child's bed
options.B: Resting lightly on the bottom mattress to reduce tension
options.C: Anchored securely to the vertical legs of the cot
options.D: Hanging freely without touching the floor or bed frame

explanation: Weights must always hang completely free so they can pull correctly on the infant's limbs without interference. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h3)

question: Where should the infant's buttocks be positioned during proper gallows traction?

options.A: Pressed firmly against the mattress surface
options.B: Hovering just slightly above the mattress
options.C: Resting on a rolled pillow for extra comfort
options.D: Suspended halfway up the vertical poles

explanation: The infant's own body weight creates the counter-traction needed, which only works if their bottom is lifted slightly off the bed. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h3)

question: How often should you check the blood circulation and nerve function of a child in traction?

options.A: Every twenty-four hours
options.B: Every two to four hours
options.C: Only when the child cries
options.D: Once every shift change

explanation: Frequent checks every two to four hours help catch poor blood flow or nerve pressure early before permanent damage happens. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which sign shows poor blood circulation in the toes of a child in traction?

options.A: Spontaneous wiggling of toes in response to sounds
options.B: Pink nail beds with immediate color return after pressure release
options.C: Capillary refill time taking longer than three seconds
options.D: Warm skin temperature across the entire foot

explanation: A slow capillary refill time means blood is not flowing well to the toes, often because the bandages are wrapped too tightly. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h4)

question: How should you change bed sheets for an infant in gallows traction?

options.A: Roll the infant firmly onto their side to pull sheets away
options.B: Disconnect the weights temporarily to lay the child flat
options.C: Lift the child completely out of the bed by their ankles
options.D: Change the linen from top to bottom without rolling the child

explanation: Rolling the infant can move the broken bone out of place. Bed sheets are changed from top to bottom while the child stays suspended. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why is changing wet diapers quickly so important for an infant in gallows traction?

options.A: Stool odor attracts flies that carry dangerous hospital infections
options.B: Moisture and stool can loosen traction tapes and damage the skin
options.C: Saturated diapers cause the traction ropes to snap under tension
options.D: Wet diapers add too much extra weight to the suspension system

explanation: Urine and feces soften the adhesive tapes used in traction and can quickly break down sensitive infant skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a common problem linked to gallows traction?

options.A: Respiratory congestion from staying still
options.B: Skin breakdown and pressure sores
options.C: Increased pressure inside the skull
options.D: Circulatory problems in the toes

explanation: Gallows traction affects the lower body and legs, so it does not cause changes to intracranial pressure inside the head. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h6)

question: What should you do immediately if an infant's toes become cold, blue, and have no pulse?

options.A: Massage the lower legs firmly to break up any blood clots
options.B: Apply a warm water bottle directly to the toes to warm them
options.C: Notify the doctor and prepare to adjust or remove the traction
options.D: Increase the hanging weight to pull blood down into the feet

explanation: Cold, blue toes mean the blood supply is blocked. This is an emergency that requires medical help and loosening of the tight bandages. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h6)

question: How can you best help parents cope with the stress of seeing their baby in traction?

options.A: Tell parents to stay away from the ward so the baby stops crying
options.B: Discourage asking questions so the medical team can work undisturbed
options.C: Explain the purpose of the traction and involve them in daily care
options.D: Reassure them that infants never experience pain during traction

explanation: Teaching parents what is happening and letting them help with care builds their confidence and lowers their stress. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h7)

question: Why are hanging toys placed where the infant can see them?

options.A: To provide entertainment and distract the child from fussing
options.B: To block bright hospital lights from shining into the baby's eyes
options.C: To weigh down the overhead frame so it remains stable
options.D: To test whether the infant has normal vision and eye movement

explanation: Hanging toys keep immobile babies busy and happy, which helps reduce crying while they are suspended in bed. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying skull traction?

options.A: To increase blood flow to the brain
options.B: To lower intracranial pressure in head trauma
options.C: To prevent pressure ulcers on the occipital region
options.D: To align and stabilize cervical spine injuries

explanation: Skull traction pulls directly on the skull to straighten and steady broken or dislocated neck bones. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h1)

question: How does skull traction protect the spinal cord from further harm?

options.A: By numbing nerve pathways to block pain signals to the brain
options.B: By completely eliminating the need for future spinal surgery
options.C: By stopping muscle spasms and restoring proper bone alignment
options.D: By increasing cerebrospinal fluid production around the injury

explanation: Pulling forces counteract tight neck muscles that pull bones out of place, keeping the spinal cord safe from pinching. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h1)

question: A patient with which condition is most likely to need skull traction?

options.A: Cervical spine fracture
options.B: Lumbar disc herniation
options.C: Fractured femur shaft
options.D: Acute appendicitis

explanation: Skull traction is specifically designed for injuries located in the neck portion of the vertebral column. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is skull traction applied before some neck surgeries?

options.A: To shrink swollen soft tissues around the wound
options.B: To clear bacterial infections from the spinal canal
options.C: To test if the patient is allergic to metal pins
options.D: To realign displaced bones into the correct position

explanation: Pre-operative traction pulls the spine straight so the surgeon has a better starting point for fusion. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which skull traction device uses spring-loaded pins to monitor safe pressure?

options.A: Halo vest system
options.B: Bucks traction boot
options.C: Gardner-Wells tongs
options.D: Crutchfield tongs

explanation: Gardner-Wells tongs have an indicator to show when the correct tightening pressure has been reached. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is a major advantage of the halo vest over traditional tongs?

options.A: It completely eliminates the risk of pin site infection
options.B: It does not require any pins to penetrate the skin
options.C: It requires no special nursing assessments after placement
options.D: It allows the patient to get out of bed and walk around

explanation: The body jacket secures the ring, permitting mobility unlike bed-bound tong setups. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h3)

question: What equipment must be kept at the bedside before applying skull traction?

options.A: A complete blood transfusion setup
options.B: Continuous renal replacement therapy
options.C: Suction and bag-valve-mask ventilation
options.D: A standard wheelchair and walker

explanation: Respiratory compromise can happen suddenly during cervical manipulation, requiring emergency airway support. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why is baseline neurological assessment important before skull traction starts?

options.A: To detect any changes in nerve function after the procedure begins
options.B: To prove the patient is mentally competent to sign financial forms
options.C: To determine if the patient requires general anesthesia in the theatre
options.D: To calculate the exact amount of weight needed for the pulley system

explanation: Knowing the patient's starting neurology helps nurses quickly identify if spinal alignment affects nerve pathways. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h4)

question: Where must traction weights be positioned at all times?

options.A: Supported by a small stool placed under the bed
options.B: Tied tightly to the headboard of the hospital bed
options.C: Resting securely on the bottom mattress frame
options.D: Hanging freely without touching the floor or bed

explanation: Weights must hang completely free so the correct pulling force is continuously maintained. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the main role of the nurse while the doctor places skull tongs?

options.A: Drilling the small pilot holes into the patient's outer skull
options.B: Holding the head in neutral alignment to prevent movement
options.C: Administering general anesthesia through an intravenous line
options.D: Tightening the pin screws to the manufacturer pressure limit

explanation: Maintaining a steady, straight head position protects the damaged spine while the device is secured. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h5)

question: How often should neurovascular checks be performed on a patient in skull traction?

options.A: Only when the patient complains of pain
options.B: Every two to four hours
options.C: Every fifteen minutes for the first week
options.D: Once a day during morning care

explanation: Frequent checks catch early signs of nerve compression or poor circulation in the limbs. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h6)

question: What should a nurse do if a traction rope slips out of the pulley groove?

options.A: Lift the patient's head off the bed to relieve the tension
options.B: Realign the rope in the pulley without changing the weight position
options.C: Tighten the skull pins further to make up for the lost force
options.D: Remove all the weights permanently until the doctor arrives

explanation: Fixing the mechanical setup keeps the therapeutic pull steady and prevents sudden jolts to the neck. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h6)

question: What solution is commonly used to clean skull traction pin sites?

options.A: Warm soapy tap water and vinegar
options.B: Normal saline or chlorhexidine
options.C: Pure rubbing alcohol or spirit
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide and iodine scrub

explanation: Gentle antiseptic or saline cleanses the area without damaging healing skin tissue around the pins. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which finding at a pin site requires immediate reporting to the doctor?

options.A: Firm skin tightly surrounding the pin
options.B: A small amount of clear dried serum
options.C: Purulent drainage and local warmth
options.D: Absence of pain around the metal site

explanation: Pus and heat are classic signs of localized infection that could spread to the bone. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the FIRST action a nurse must take if a skull traction pin detaches?

options.A: Remove the remaining three pins to keep the skull balanced
options.B: Lower the head of the bed flat to rest the patient
options.C: Manually stabilize the head and neck in neutral alignment
options.D: Run to the nurses station to find the attending surgeon

explanation: Protecting the cervical spine from sudden movement takes priority when mechanical traction fails. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h8)

question: Which complication is most critical to monitor for in high cervical spine injuries?

options.A: Inability to move the lower legs only
options.B: Severe chronic lower back pain
options.C: High fever due to a urinary infection
options.D: Respiratory distress and failure

explanation: Injuries high up in the neck can paralyze breathing muscles, making airway compromise an emergency. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T11#GNS221_U1_T11_h8)

question: What is the primary mechanical action of cervical traction?

options.A: Rotating the head continuously
options.B: Compressing the cervical vertebrae together
options.C: Freezing the neck muscles using cold therapy
options.D: Applying a pulling force to the neck

explanation: Cervical traction works by applying a controlled pulling force to stretch soft tissues and relieve spinal pressure. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is cervical traction applied before some spinal surgeries?

options.A: To increase blood pressure in the brain
options.B: To permanently fuse the vertebrae without surgery
options.C: To numb the neck skin completely
options.D: To align fractures and reduce nerve compression

explanation: Pulling forces help realign displaced bones and take pressure off nerves prior to a formal operation. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which traction method uses metal pins inserted directly into the skull?

options.A: Skin traction
options.B: Pelvic traction
options.C: Skeletal traction
options.D: Buck's traction

explanation: Skeletal traction involves drilling pins or tongs into the skull bones to bear heavy pulling loads. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h2)

question: Skin traction is restricted to lighter weights mainly to prevent what complication?

options.A: Skin breakdown on the chin and scalp
options.B: Fracture of the skull bones
options.C: Infection inside the brain tissue
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the arms

explanation: Because a head halter applies pressure directly to the skin, heavy weights will cause tissue ischemia and breakdown. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which condition is a clear contraindication for cervical traction?

options.A: Muscle spasm in the neck
options.B: Acute torticollis
options.C: Cervical disc herniation
options.D: Severe osteoporosis

explanation: Fragile bones in severe osteoporosis can easily fracture or fail under the pulling force of traction. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h3)

question: A patient with a spinal cord tumor should avoid cervical traction because pulling forces can cause what?

options.A: Worsening of neurological damage
options.B: Rapid shrinking of the tumor
options.C: Severe infection of the skin
options.D: High fever and chills

explanation: Traction on a compromised or unstable spine containing a tumor can shift structures and increase spinal cord compression. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h3)

question: Where should the traction weights be positioned during therapy?

options.A: Tucked underneath the mattress
options.B: Hanging freely above the floor
options.C: Placed on the patient's chest
options.D: Resting partially on the bed frame

explanation: Weights must hang free so the intended amount of pulling force is continuously and evenly applied. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h4)

question: What happens if a traction rope catches on the bed frame?

options.A: The pulling force is interrupted or altered
options.B: The traction automatically becomes stronger
options.C: The skin halter falls off the head
options.D: The patient's blood pressure drops instantly

explanation: Friction from the bed frame interferes with the pulley system, reducing the effective weight applied to the neck. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which assessment is essential for a patient in cervical traction?

options.A: Bowel sounds in all four abdominal quadrants
options.B: Daily weight measurements using a standing scale
options.C: Upper extremity motor function and sensation
options.D: Visual acuity and peripheral vision fields

explanation: Monitoring arms and hands helps detect early signs of nerve compression or spinal cord injury. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why must the nurse frequently check the skin beneath a skin traction halter?

options.A: To check if hair is growing too fast
options.B: To apply new layers of surgical paint
options.C: To catch early signs of pressure sores
options.D: To measure the exact head circumference

explanation: Continuous friction and pressure from halters can rapidly break down delicate facial and scalp skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is the primary danger associated with skeletal traction pin sites?

options.A: Permanent change in hair color
options.B: Excessive hair growth around the pins
options.C: Bone infection like osteomyelitis
options.D: Rapid healing of the bone hole

explanation: Pins penetrate the skin directly into bone, creating a direct route for bacteria to cause deep infection. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which action is required when performing pin site care?

options.A: Scrubbing the metal pins with a stiff wire brush
options.B: Using strict aseptic technique to prevent germs
options.C: Leaving the crusts undisturbed without cleaning
options.D: Applying thick oil to seal the wound completely

explanation: Aseptic technique stops external bacteria from entering the open pin tract and causing infection. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h6)

question: What emergency action must be taken if traction weights must be removed immediately?

options.A: Leave the room to find a doctor first
options.B: Manually stabilize the patient's head
options.C: Turn the patient onto their stomach
options.D: Raise the head of the bed to ninety degrees

explanation: Manual stabilization prevents uncontrolled, dangerous movement of an unstable cervical spine when traction is lost. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which finding requires immediate emergency nursing intervention in a traction patient?

options.A: Boredom due to prolonged bed rest
options.B: Mild itching under the chin strap
options.C: Sudden respiratory distress and decline
options.D: Slight redness on the back of the scalp

explanation: Respiratory failure indicates possible upper cervical cord swelling or airway compromise requiring urgent intervention. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h7)

question: What should a patient wear after cervical traction is discontinued?

options.A: A soft cotton scarf only
options.B: A metal halo ring without vest
options.C: A prescribed neck collar
options.D: A heavy plaster body jacket

explanation: Cervical collars provide temporary external support while neck muscles regain strength after traction removal. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h8)

question: Why is patient education crucial during the discontinuation phase of traction?

options.A: To help the patient adjust the traction weights alone
options.B: To prove the treatment was completely unsuccessful
options.C: To train the patient on how to clean metal pins
options.D: To prevent accidental reinjury from sudden neck movement

explanation: Once traction is removed, the unsupported spine is vulnerable until surrounding muscles heal and strengthen. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T12#GNS221_U1_T12_h8)

question: What defines an active range of motion exercise?

options.A: Resistance is applied while the patient holds the joint totally still.
options.B: The nurse moves the joint completely through its motion for the patient.
options.C: The patient moves the joint independently using their own muscles.
options.D: A mechanical machine forces the joint to bend and straighten.

explanation: Active range of motion relies strictly on the patient's own muscular contraction without external assistance. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h1)

question: A patient is performing AROM exercises in bed. What does this movement primarily evaluate?

options.A: Muscle strength and joint mobility
options.B: Peripheral nerve conduction velocity only
options.C: Kidney filtration rate and electrolyte balance
options.D: Cardiovascular endurance and lung capacity

explanation: Moving joints independently demonstrates the current capability of both the muscular and skeletal systems. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h1)

question: The primary circulatory benefit of active range of motion is...

options.A: increasing total red blood cell production in bone marrow.
options.B: stopping fluid retention in the peritoneal cavity.
options.C: lowering systemic blood pressure instantly during exercise.
options.D: preventing blood clots by enhancing venous return.

explanation: Active muscle contractions compress blood vessels, pushing blood back toward the heart and preventing stasis. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why is encouraging AROM preferred over passive exercise when a patient is able?

options.A: It takes significantly less time for the nursing staff.
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any pain medication.
options.C: It maintains muscle tone and active user independence.
options.D: It requires zero effort or concentration from the client.

explanation: Using their own muscles keeps fibers strong and gives patients a sense of control over their healing. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h2)

question: Which clinical situation is a clear contraindication for AROM?

options.A: A newly diagnosed, unhealed bone fracture in the limb
options.B: Chronic stable hypertension controlled with daily tablets
options.C: A healed surgical scar from a minor procedure last year
options.D: Mild generalized fatigue after a restful night of sleep

explanation: Moving an unhealed fracture disrupts bone healing and causes severe tissue damage. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h3)

question: A client with a fresh abdominal surgical wound asks to start arm exercises. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Allow unrestricted movement since arms are far from the abdomen.
options.B: Refuse the request permanently without notifying anyone.
options.C: Check the primary health provider order before permitting exercise.
options.D: Force the patient to walk around the ward instead.

explanation: Abdominal movements can stress core surgical sites, so medical clearance is mandatory before starting activity. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is a necessary action before initiating AROM exercises?

options.A: Place the patient in a prone position facing the mattress.
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake for the next six hours.
options.C: Assess the patient's current pain level and baseline vitals.
options.D: Administer a strong dose of intravenous narcotic painkiller.

explanation: Checking vitals and pain ensures the patient is stable enough to tolerate physical activity safely. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why is adjusting the bed to a proper height important for the nurse?

options.A: It prevents back strain and awkward posture during care.
options.B: It directly lowers the environmental temperature in the room.
options.C: It speeds up the rate at which muscles contract.
options.D: It keeps the patient from falling asleep mid-exercise.

explanation: Proper body mechanics protect the nurse from musculoskeletal injuries while assisting patients. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h4)

question: How many repetitions are typically performed for each joint movement during routine AROM?

options.A: Zero, movements are done only once
options.B: Fifty to one hundred repetitions
options.C: Two to five repetitions
options.D: Exactly twenty-five continuous repetitions

explanation: A small number of repetitions prevents exhaustion while maintaining joint flexibility. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h5)

question: In what order should AROM exercises generally be conducted across the body?

options.A: Starting at the toes and moving up to the head
options.B: Systematically from the head down to the toes
options.C: Randomly picking any joint that looks stiffest
options.D: Only focusing on the right side of the body

explanation: A head-to-toe approach ensures no joints are accidentally missed during the routine assessment and exercise session. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h5)

question: What should the nurse do immediately if a patient feels sharp pain during AROM?

options.A: Ignore the complaint and finish the remaining repetitions.
options.B: Stop the exercise immediately and let the patient rest.
options.C: Push harder through the pain to break up scar tissue.
options.D: Ask the patient to stand up and walk around the room.

explanation: Sharp pain indicates potential tissue injury, requiring an immediate halt to the activity. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which sign is an indication to pause exercises due to systemic intolerance?

options.A: Mild muscle warmth from normal blood flow
options.B: Sudden diaphoresis and shortness of breath
options.C: Steady and even breathing throughout the routine
options.D: Calm facial expression during limb movement

explanation: Sweating and breathlessness show the body is under excessive cardiorespiratory stress. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to include when documenting AROM exercises?

options.A: The patient's tolerance and any reported pain
options.B: The weather outside during the nursing shift
options.C: The brand name of the soap used for handwashing
options.D: The exact cost of the hospital bed equipment

explanation: Documenting tolerance and pain tracks recovery progress and ensures safe ongoing care. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why is timely documentation of physical exercise important for the healthcare team?

options.A: It allows billing departments to calculate room rental fees.
options.B: It provides continuity of care and tracks functional progress.
options.C: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers entirely.
options.D: It proves the nurse completed their paperwork to avoid fines.

explanation: Accurate records let all team members see how well the patient is responding to mobility interventions. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T2#GNS221_U1_T2_h7)

question: What happens to the patient's muscles during passive range of motion exercises?

options.A: They undergo isometric strengthening contractions
options.B: They tense up to protect the injured joint
options.C: They remain completely relaxed and do not work
options.D: They contract forcefully to assist the movement

explanation: During PROM, the patient exerts no effort and the muscles remain relaxed while an outside force moves the joint. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h1)

question: Who supplies the energy needed to move a joint during PROM?

options.A: An external force or caregiver
options.B: Involuntary reflex muscle spasms
options.C: An electrical muscle stimulator machine
options.D: The patient's own skeletal muscles

explanation: Because the patient is passive, a nurse or therapist must supply all the mechanical force to move the limb. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h1)

question: A primary clinical purpose of performing PROM is to prevent which condition?

options.A: Bone fractures
options.B: Muscle hypertrophy
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Joint contractures

explanation: Moving joints passively keeps tissues pliable, stopping them from permanently shortening into contractures. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why does moving a joint passively help nourish its cartilage?

options.A: It pumps synovial fluid throughout the joint space
options.B: It stimulates calcium deposits to form on the bone ends
options.C: It triggers hormonal growth factor release in the marrow
options.D: It increases direct blood supply to avascular cartilage

explanation: Articular cartilage lacks its own blood vessels and relies on the movement of synovial fluid generated during joint motion for nutrition. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which condition is an absolute contraindication for performing passive range of motion?

options.A: An unstable recent bone fracture
options.B: Chronic controlled high blood pressure
options.C: A healed scar from previous surgery
options.D: Mild generalized muscle weakness

explanation: Moving a limb with an unstable fracture causes further tissue damage and prevents proper bone healing. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h3)

question: What should a nurse do when encountering resistance during PROM?

options.A: Stop immediately and do not force the movement
options.B: Administer a strong painkiller and continue the routine
options.C: Ask another nurse to help apply more physical force
options.D: Push harder through the barrier to break adhesions

explanation: Forcing a joint past its natural resistance or pain threshold risks tearing muscles, ligaments, or joint capsules. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h3)

question: How should the nurse hold a limb while performing passive joint exercises?

options.A: Supporting both sides of the joint securely
options.B: Applying pressure directly on the joint line
options.C: Holding only the very tip of the distal digit
options.D: Suspended freely without any physical support

explanation: Supporting the limb both above and below the joint prevents undue stress and protects the bone and ligaments. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h4)

question: A nurse prepares to exercise a patient's leg. What is the correct way to handle the clothing and bed linens?

options.A: Expose only the specific leg being exercised
options.B: Remove all bed covers to see the full body alignment
options.C: Leave all blankets completely closed over the patient
options.D: Undress the patient fully to promote total body air flow

explanation: Dignity and privacy require uncovering only the immediate body part undergoing the physical procedure. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h4)

question: When exercising a patient's lower extremity, where should the nurse place their hands for support?

options.A: Under the heel and beneath the knee
options.B: Around the middle of the thigh bone only
options.C: Directly on top of the kneecap and toes
options.D: Tightly wrapped around the ankle joint line

explanation: Placing hands under the heel and knee provides safe cradling and control of the entire lower limb. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the correct directional approach when performing a full routine of PROM exercises?

options.A: Focusing solely on the dominant arm and leg of the patient
options.B: Starting with the toes and moving randomly upward
options.C: Exercising only the joints that look stiff to the eye
options.D: Systematically moving from one major joint to the next

explanation: A systematic head-to-toe or proximal-to-distal approach ensures no joint is accidentally missed during the care session. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the most reliable sign of distress in a non-communicative patient during PROM?

options.A: An increase in overall body weight
options.B: Normal resting respiratory rate patterns
options.C: Facial grimacing and muscle guarding
options.D: A decrease in room temperature sweating

explanation: When patients cannot speak, facial expressions and tensing of the muscles show that movement is causing pain. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h6)

question: A patient whispers that their shoulder hurts halfway through an arm exercise. What action should follow?

options.A: Double the speed to finish the routine much faster
options.B: Ignore the comment and finish the remaining repetitions
options.C: Push through the pain to loosen up the joint capsule
options.D: Stop the movement immediately and assess the joint

explanation: Patient complaints of pain mean the exercise must halt to prevent injury to the underlying joint structures. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to record in the nursing notes after performing PROM?

options.A: The personal visiting hours of family members
options.B: Any patient complaints or signs of discomfort
options.C: The exact brand of soap used during morning bath
options.D: The dietary menu selected by the kitchen staff

explanation: Documenting how the patient tolerated the procedure and noting any pain is vital for ongoing clinical evaluation. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why is prompt reporting of new joint swelling after PROM important?

options.A: It means the patient is ready for full independent discharge
options.B: It signals that the room temperature is too high
options.C: It proves the exercises successfully increased muscle mass
options.D: It could indicate acute tissue injury or micro-trauma

explanation: Unexplained swelling or redness after movement can signify a tear, strain, or other injury requiring medical review. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T3#GNS221_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the main goal of physiotherapy in nursing care?

options.A: Giving IV medications
options.B: Performing major surgery
options.C: Restoring physical movement and mobility
options.D: Checking for broken bones

explanation: Physiotherapy helps patients recover and maintain their ability to move around safely. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is a common physical problem caused by staying in bed for too long?

options.A: Faster nerve repair
options.B: Loss of muscle size and flexibility
options.C: Stronger heart endurance
options.D: Stronger bones

explanation: When muscles are not used, they weaken and joints become stiff very quickly. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which type of exercise involves the nurse moving a patient's joints because the patient cannot move them alone?

options.A: Weight training
options.B: Isometric muscle tightening
options.C: Passive range of motion exercises
options.D: Active-assistive stretching

explanation: Passive exercises mean the nurse moves the limbs for the patient to keep the joints flexible. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h2)

question: When are isometric exercises most useful?

options.A: For gaining heavy body weight
options.B: For running long distances
options.C: To prevent muscle wasting without bending joints
options.D: For stretching tight ligaments

explanation: Isometric exercises tighten muscles without moving the joints, which is helpful when movement is restricted. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is cold therapy usually used for in fresh injuries?

options.A: Increasing blood flow
options.B: Softening scar tissue
options.C: Relaxing deep muscle spasms
options.D: Reducing swelling and numbing pain

explanation: Cold packs narrow blood vessels, which helps stop fluid buildup and numbs the pain around new injuries. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h3)

question: When should heat therapy definitely NOT be used?

options.A: Over fresh bleeding or new swelling
options.B: To relieve general muscle stiffness
options.C: During chronic back pain
options.D: Before stretching stiff joints

explanation: Heat increases blood flow, which makes fresh bleeding and acute swelling worse. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why should a patient let their legs dangle at the bedside before standing up?

options.A: To strengthen thigh muscles
options.B: To measure leg length
options.C: To check for leg swelling
options.D: To prevent sudden dizziness from low blood pressure

explanation: Sitting on the edge of the bed helps the blood vessels adjust so the patient does not feel dizzy from standing too fast. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h4)

question: A patient is learning to walk with a new walker. Where should the nurse stand?

options.A: Directly behind the walker frame
options.B: Far across the room
options.C: Directly in front walking backward
options.D: Slightly behind and to the side holding a gait belt

explanation: This position lets the nurse safely hold the gait belt to steady the patient if they slip. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h4)

question: How often should bedridden patients be turned to protect their skin?

options.A: Every 2 hours
options.B: Every 6 hours
options.C: Only when they ask
options.D: Once per shift

explanation: Turning a patient every two hours relieves pressure and prevents pressure sores. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of a footboard in bed care?

options.A: To prevent blood clots
options.B: To prevent back sores
options.C: To prevent foot drop
options.D: To stop knee dislocation

explanation: A footboard keeps the feet in a proper upright position so the calf muscles do not shorten permanently. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h5)

question: Who is mainly responsible for assessing complex movement problems in a hospital?

options.A: The attending doctor
options.B: The ward staff nurse
options.C: The hospital pharmacist
options.D: The physical therapist

explanation: Physical therapists have specialized training to evaluate and treat movement and muscle issues. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is the nurse's main role regarding physical therapy?

options.A: Taking over the therapist's job on weekends
options.B: Redesigning the rehab schedule
options.C: Changing electrical therapy settings
options.D: Encouraging exercises during daily ward routines

explanation: Since nurses spend the most time with patients, they help patients practice their therapy movements throughout the day. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which home change is most important to prevent patient falls after leaving the hospital?

options.A: Painting bedroom walls bright colors
options.B: Removing loose rugs and clearing pathways
options.C: Buying heavy wooden tables
options.D: Installing ceiling fans

explanation: Loose rugs and clutter are common tripping hazards for patients who are unsteady on their feet. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why is family involvement important when planning for a patient to go home with mobility needs?

options.A: To prevent family injury and ensure safe moving at home
options.B: To take over all legal medical duties
options.C: To check surgical wounds alone
options.D: To pay for expensive hospital gear

explanation: Teaching relatives proper lifting techniques keeps them safe from back injuries while helping the patient move around. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the chemical name for the powder used to make Plaster of Paris?

options.A: Sodium chloride dihydrate
options.B: Calcium carbonate anhydrous
options.C: Calcium sulfate hemihydrate
options.D: Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate

explanation: Plaster of Paris is produced by heating gypsum to create calcium sulfate hemihydrate powder. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why does a curing Plaster of Paris cast feel warm to the touch?

options.A: Body heat is trapped inside the wet cotton padding
options.B: Electric warmers are used to speed up drying
options.C: Friction from bandage wrapping creates thermal energy
options.D: An exothermic hydration reaction releases heat

explanation: Mixing the powder with water causes a chemical reaction that naturally produces heat as it hardens. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h1)

question: The primary clinical purpose of applying a Plaster of Paris cast is what?

options.A: Immobilize fractured bones to promote healing
options.B: Increase local blood circulation in limbs
options.C: Prevent muscle hypertrophy during bed rest
options.D: Deliver topical antibiotics to open wounds

explanation: Casts hold broken bone ends steady to allow proper alignment and callus formation. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h2)

question: A child with clubfoot is brought to the clinic for serial casting. What is the main goal?

options.A: Protect the skin from insect bites
options.B: Treat a sudden bone infection
options.C: Correct congenital deformities gradually
options.D: Keep the infant from crawling early

explanation: Serial casting uses the rigid support of POP to gradually stretch tight soft tissues and correct skeletal malformations. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the function of the stockinette placed before the plaster roll?

options.A: Protect the skin from friction and irritation
options.B: Absorb excess heat generated by the water
options.C: Add structural weight and strength to the limb
options.D: Speed up the drying time of the outer cast

explanation: The stockinette acts as a soft barrier between the rough plaster material and the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why should a nurse use tepid water instead of hot water for soaking POP bandages?

options.A: Cold water makes the plaster completely dissolve into liquid
options.B: Tepid water is required to activate the chemical coloring agents
options.C: Hot water causes the plaster to set too fast and generates excess heat
options.D: Hot water prevents the plaster from ever hardening at all

explanation: Water temperature dictates setting speed; excessively hot water causes rapid hardening and risks burning the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h3)

question: How should a nurse submerge a Plaster of Paris bandage into the water basin?

options.A: Soak it overnight in a sealed plastic container
options.B: Hold it vertically under a running tap for seconds
options.C: Immerse it horizontally until bubbling ceases
options.D: Boil the roll in water before wrapping the limb

explanation: Horizontal immersion allows water to penetrate the core evenly, indicated by the cessation of air bubbles. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why must the operator avoid using fingertips to mold a fresh wet cast?

options.A: Indentations can press into the skin and cause pressure sores
options.B: Pressure from fingertips makes the cast crack in half
options.C: Natural oils on fingers dissolve the wet plaster material
options.D: Fingerprints permanently ruin the shiny outer finish

explanation: Using the palms of the hands instead of fingertips prevents localized pressure points from forming inside the hardening cast. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h4)

question: What are the key clinical indicators checked during a neurovascular assessment of a casted limb?

options.A: Muscle tone, pupil reaction, reflexes, posture
options.B: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis
options.C: Temperature, respiration, blood pressure, pulse
options.D: Skin turgor, bowel sounds, urine output, jaundice

explanation: These five clinical signs help nurses detect early compartment syndrome or circulation blockage. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h5)
